chapters.heading: CHAPTER 16 - A Life Emptied Out as a Sign
chapters.title: A Life Emptied Out as a Sign
keyNotes: Jeremiah is forbidden to marry or father children in that place - not as asceticism, but as a living sign: a generation is coming whose sons and daughters will die unlamented and unburied (Jeremiah 16:1-4).
He is forbidden to enter the house of mourning, because Yahweh has withdrawn His shalom from this people - and with it His loving kindness and tender mercies (Jeremiah 16:5-7).
He is equally forbidden the house of feasting: the voice of mirth and gladness, of bridegroom and bride, will cease before their own eyes and in their own days (Jeremiah 16:8-9).

When the people ask "What is our iniquity?" the answer is not vague - their fathers forsook Yahweh and walked after other gods, and this generation has done worse than their fathers (Jeremiah 16:10-13).

In the middle of the sentence comes an astonishing promise: a day when Israel's defining testimony will no longer be the exodus from Egypt but a greater gathering out of the land of the north (Jeremiah 16:14-15).
Fishermen and hunters will be sent - a total, inescapable search - because Yahweh's eyes are on all their ways and their iniquity is not concealed from Him (Jeremiah 16:16-18).
The chapter ends with the nations themselves coming from the ends of the earth, confessing that their fathers inherited nothing but lies, and learning that His name is Yahweh (Jeremiah 16:19-21).

intro: Yahweh has taken things from Jeremiah before. In chapter 13 it was a linen waistcloth. In chapter 15 it was his peace and his place in ordinary company. Here He takes his future. No wife. No children. No attendance at funerals. No attendance at weddings. The prophet himself becomes the object lesson, and the lesson is loneliness.

Each prohibition is explained, and the explanations are worse than the prohibitions. Do not marry, because the children born in this place are going to die of disease and famine and lie unburied. Do not enter a house of mourning, because peace has been withdrawn and there will be no one left to comfort or to bury. Do not sit down to eat and drink at a feast, because the voice of the bridegroom and the bride is going to stop in this land within living memory. A man's whole social life is cancelled, and each cancellation is a forecast.

There is a hard exchange in verses 10 through 13 that is worth watching. The people ask, reasonably enough on their own terms, what they have done - what is our iniquity, what is our sin? The answer is not a list of their own offences first. It begins with their fathers, and then adds that they have done worse than their fathers, each one walking after the stubbornness of his evil heart. Inheritance is real in this book, and it is never an excuse.

But notice where the chapter goes next, because it turns without warning. In the middle of a passage about deportation, Yahweh interrupts Himself with a promise large enough to retire Israel's oldest piece of testimony. The days are coming when nobody will say "as Yahweh lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt," but rather "who brought them up out of the north country." The exodus - the founding story, the thing every generation was commanded to rehearse - is going to be superseded by something people have not seen yet.

And then, further out still, verse 19: the nations will come to Him from the ends of the earth and say that their fathers inherited nothing but lies. The vision keeps widening the further into the judgement it goes.
The God who empties a house can fill a nation. In this book judgement is never the last word; it is the ground being cleared for a homecoming that will be worth more than the story it replaces.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 17 - The Engraved Heart, the Two Trees, and the Sabbath Gate
chapters.title: The Engraved Heart, the Two Trees, and the Sabbath Gate
keyNotes: Judah's sin is written with an iron pen and a diamond point - engraved on the tablet of their heart and on the horns of their altars. Their worship itself carries the record of their guilt (Jeremiah 17:1-4).
Two men are set side by side. Cursed is the man who trusts in man and relies on strength of flesh: he is a shrub in the desert who will not even recognize good when it arrives (Jeremiah 17:5-6).
Blessed is the man whose confidence is in Yahweh: a tree planted by the waters, roots spread to the river, green in the heat and fruitful in the year of drought (Jeremiah 17:7-8).
"The heart is deceitful above all things" is not despair but diagnosis - and it is immediately answered by the One who says, "I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart" (Jeremiah 17:9-10).
Riches gotten wrongly are like a partridge sitting on eggs she did not lay - they leave in the middle of life, and the end is folly (Jeremiah 17:11).
Those who forsake Yahweh, the spring of living waters, are written in the earth - a name in dust, erased by the next wind (Jeremiah 17:12-13).
Jeremiah prays the prayer that puts everything in the right hands: "Heal me, O Yahweh, and I will be healed. Save me, and I will be saved" (Jeremiah 17:14-18).

The chapter closes at the city gates with a concrete test of covenant loyalty: bear no burden on the Sabbath. Obedience means an enduring city; refusal means an unquenched fire in its gates (Jeremiah 17:19-27).

intro: This is the chapter where Jeremiah stops describing a nation and starts describing a person - any person, including whoever is reading it. Sin engraved with an iron pen and a diamond point on the tablet of the heart, which is deliberate imagery: the same word used for the tablets at Sinai, with the writing now on the wrong surface.

Then the two trees, and the difference between them is entirely a matter of root systems. The man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm is like a shrub in the desert, standing in a salt land where nobody lives, unable to recognise good when it arrives. The man who trusts in Yahweh is a tree planted by waters that spreads its roots by the river - and the point of that picture is not that it flourishes in good conditions. It is that it does not notice when heat comes, and is not anxious in the year of drought, because the water it is drawing on has nothing to do with the weather.

In the middle sits the verse most people have heard quoted and few have heard finished. "The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?" That is a question, not a verdict, and the very next breath answers it: I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart. The passage is not a counsel of despair about human self-knowledge. It is a statement that Someone else has access.

There is a line here that anyone who has ever wanted something badly should hold onto, and it is oddly practical. A partridge that hatches eggs she did not lay is the image, and the application is a man who gets rich unjustly and loses it in the middle of his days. The chapter is not squeamish about money.

Then the chapter does something unexpected. It does not end in introspection. It ends at a gate, with a wagon, on a Sabbath. Stand in the gate, tell them to carry no burden through it, do not bring loads out of your houses. The heart that Yahweh searches turns out to be tested not by feeling but by whether a man unloads the cart.

That is the chapter's real argument, and it is easy to miss because the middle of it is so quotable. The test of where a person's trust rests is rarely dramatic. It usually looks like an ordinary decision on an ordinary seventh day, about goods, in public, where everyone can see whether you meant it.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 18 - The Potter's House, the Refusal, and the Plot
chapters.title: The Potter's House, the Refusal, and the Plot
keyNotes: Jeremiah is sent down to the potter's house to receive a word he could not have received in the temple - the sermon is the workshop itself (Jeremiah 18:1-3).
The vessel is marred in the potter's hand, and the potter does not discard the clay. He makes it again, another vessel, as it seemed good to him to make it (Jeremiah 18:4).

The principle is then stated plainly: Yahweh's sovereignty over nations is real and it is responsive. Declared judgment is withdrawn when a nation turns; declared blessing is withdrawn when it rebels (Jeremiah 18:5-10).
The offer is issued in the plainest possible terms - "return now, everyone from his evil way" - and is met with the most chilling answer in the book: "It is in vain" (Jeremiah 18:11-12).
Yahweh points to the natural world to expose the unnatural thing: the snow of Lebanon does not fail, the cold mountain waters do not dry up, but His people have forgotten Him (Jeremiah 18:13-15).
They have been made to stumble out of the ancient paths into byways - roads that were never built up, leading to a land of astonishment and hissing (Jeremiah 18:15-17).
The response to the message is a conspiracy against the messenger: priest, wise man, and prophet agree that Jeremiah can simply be struck with the tongue and ignored (Jeremiah 18:18).
Jeremiah answers with raw, unedited lament - evil repaid for good, a pit dug for the very soul that stood before Yahweh to speak good on their behalf (Jeremiah 18:19-23).

intro: Yahweh does not explain this one in advance. He sends Jeremiah on an errand - down the hill, to a workshop, to watch a man work - and lets the sight do the teaching.

What Jeremiah sees is not a potter smashing a failed pot. He sees a potter whose hands never leave the clay. The vessel is marred in his hand, the wheel keeps turning, and the same hands begin again and make it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to make it. That is the image Yahweh chooses for Himself before He says a single word about judgement.

And it matters enormously that what He says next is conditional in both directions. If a nation I have spoken against turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster I intended. If a nation I have spoken good of does evil, I will relent of the good. The clay in this passage is not passive. It answers, and the answer is taken into account.

Which is why Judah's reply is so devastating. "It is in vain" - or, more literally, there is no hope, we will walk after our own plans. They do not dispute the diagnosis. They do not argue that the potter has no right. They simply decline. That is the sentence that turns a workshop into a courtroom.

The last section of the chapter is the fifth of Jeremiah's confessions, and it is the ugliest thing he ever says. They have dug a pit for his soul; he asks that their children be given to famine and their wives be bereaved. It sits in scripture without comment or correction. What is worth noticing is what he does not do: he does not act on any of it. He hands it over, in words, to the only one who could carry it out - which is a different thing from revenge, and is arguably the whole point of the psalms that do the same.

The tension the chapter leaves is not resolved and is not meant to be. The hand that can remake a person is the same hand that person can refuse. Sovereignty here is not fate. It is a craftsman with wet clay in his hands, waiting to see whether it will yield.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 19 - The Flask Broken in the Valley of Slaughter
chapters.title: The Flask Broken in the Valley of Slaughter
keyNotes: Jeremiah is told to buy a potter's earthen bottle - a baked, finished vessel, not wet clay - and to bring official witnesses: elders of the people and elders of the priests (Jeremiah 19:1).
The venue is the sermon. The valley of the son of Hinnom was where children had been burned; Yahweh sends His word to be preached at the scene of the crime (Jeremiah 19:2).
The charge is threefold and specific: they forsook Yahweh, they burned incense to gods they did not know, and they filled the place with the blood of innocents (Jeremiah 19:3-4).

Of child sacrifice Yahweh says something He says almost nowhere else - "which I didn't command, nor speak, which didn't even enter into my mind." It never occurred to Him to ask for this (Jeremiah 19:5).
The valley gets a new name. Topheth becomes the Valley of Slaughter - the place will be renamed by what happens in it rather than by what was worshiped there (Jeremiah 19:6).

"I will make the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem void" - their strategy sessions and alliances are the specific thing emptied out. The word for void plays on the Hebrew for the jar itself (Jeremiah 19:7).
The horrors of verses 8 and 9 are not new inventions but quotations of the covenant curses Deuteronomy had already spelled out for a besieged and unrepentant nation (Jeremiah 19:8-9).

The jar is broken in front of the witnesses. Unlike the clay in chapter 18, this vessel has been fired - it can no longer be reworked, only shattered "that can't be made whole again" (Jeremiah 19:10-11).
The rooftops are named as altars: incense to the host of heaven and drink offerings to other gods, poured out in the open air over the ordinary houses of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 19:13).

Jeremiah does not stay in the valley. He walks back up and repeats the whole thing in the temple court, where the priests will certainly hear it - which is exactly what happens next (Jeremiah 19:14-15).

intro: Read this chapter immediately after the previous one and the difference does the work. At the potter's house the clay was still on the wheel and still wet - marred, and remade by the same hands. Here Jeremiah is told to go and buy a bottle. A finished one. Baked hard in a kiln. That vessel has exactly one transformation left available to it, and it is not restoration.

Then look at where Yahweh sends him with it. Not the temple courts, not the palace gate - the valley of the son of Hinnom, ge ben-Hinnom, which centuries later contracted in Aramaic into Gehenna and became the word Yahshua used for the fire that is not quenched. Judah had turned a valley outside the city into a place where children were burned. Yahweh sends His word to that address and lets the address do half the preaching.

And He brings witnesses. Elders of the people and elders of the priests - men whose presence makes a thing official. This is not a street-corner outburst. It is a deposition, staged at the Potsherd Gate, where the city's broken pottery was thrown out.

Verse 5 deserves to be sat with, because there is almost nothing else like it in scripture. Yahweh does not merely say that child sacrifice was forbidden, or that He hates it, both of which He says elsewhere. He says it never entered His mind - the thought was not available to Him to have. Whatever else this chapter is, it is a window onto a holiness that cannot even conceive of the practice His own people had normalised and built an installation for.

The sign-act itself is brutally simple. Break the bottle in front of the witnesses and say: so will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel that cannot be made whole again. Then walk back up to the temple court and say it again to everyone there.

And the last verse names the real problem, which is not the valley. "They have made their neck stiff, that they may not hear my words." The atrocities in Hinnom were downstream of something. The stiffened neck came first, and everything else followed from it.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 20 - Fire in the Bones and Terror on Every Side
chapters.title: Fire in the Bones and Terror on Every Side
keyNotes: Pashhur son of Immer, chief officer of the temple, hears the sermon from chapter 19 and responds with violence: he strikes the prophet and locks him in the stocks in the upper gate of Benjamin (Jeremiah 20:1-2).
Jeremiah's first words on release are not a complaint but a renaming: "Yahweh has not called your name Pashhur, but Magormissabib" - Terror on Every Side (Jeremiah 20:3).
The sentence on Pashhur is exact and personal. He will watch it happen, then go to Babylon, die there, and be buried there along with everyone he comforted with lies (Jeremiah 20:4-6).

Then the chapter turns inward, and the language is almost violent. The verb behind "you have persuaded me" is used elsewhere of seduction and deception - Jeremiah says Yahweh overpowered him (Jeremiah 20:7).
The cost is constant, not occasional: "as often as I speak, I cry out" - and the word of Yahweh itself has become the reason he is mocked all day long (Jeremiah 20:8).

Verse 9 is the center of the book's inner life. He tries to quit, and cannot: the word becomes a burning fire shut up in his bones, and holding it in exhausts him more than speaking it does (Jeremiah 20:9).
The betrayal is intimate. It is not strangers but "all my familiar friends" who watch for his fall and repeat Pashhur's new name back at him as a taunt (Jeremiah 20:10).
The turn comes without transition: "But Yahweh is with me as an awesome mighty one." Faith here is not the absence of the previous verse but a decision made on top of it (Jeremiah 20:11).
He hands his case over rather than avenging it himself, appealing to the One "who sees the heart and the mind" - the same claim made about Yahweh in chapter 17 (Jeremiah 20:12).
Verse 13 is genuine praise: "Sing to Yahweh! Praise Yahweh, for he has delivered the soul of the needy." And then, five words later, the chapter falls off a cliff (Jeremiah 20:13).

The last five verses curse the day of his birth and the man who announced it. Scripture records this without correcting it, which tells us something about what may be brought to God honestly (Jeremiah 20:14-18).

intro: This is the chapter people quote and the chapter people skip, and it is the same chapter.

It opens with the first recorded physical violence against Jeremiah. Pashhur, the chief officer of the temple, strikes him and puts him in the stocks overnight at the upper gate of Benjamin - a punishment designed less to hurt than to humiliate, since the whole point of stocks is to be seen in them. When Jeremiah is released the next morning he does not go home. He renames the man. Not Pashhur, but Magor-Missabib, Terror on Every Side - a phrase that will follow this book to its last chapters, eventually aimed at Egypt and at the desert tribes.

Then comes the part that gets quoted. He decides to stop. He is finished - no more preaching, no more speaking in that name, no more standing in temple courts being hated for nothing. And he discovers that he cannot keep the resolution, because the word has become like a burning fire shut up in his bones, and holding it in turns out to be more exhausting than saying it. Anyone who has tried to walk away from something God gave them recognises verse 9 from the inside.

The part people skip is verses 14 through 18. He curses the day he was born. He curses the man who carried the happy news to his father, and wishes that man had been overthrown like the cities Yahweh did not relent over. He asks why he came out of the womb at all, to see labour and sorrow and spend his days in shame. There is no resolution afterwards. No closing verse tidies it up. The chapter simply stops there.

And the sequence refuses to behave. Verse 11: Yahweh is with me as an awesome mighty one. Verse 13: sing to Yahweh, praise Yahweh, for he has delivered the soul of the needy. Verse 14: cursed is the day I was born. That is not a man losing his faith. That is a man whose faith and whose grief are both entirely real in the same hour, and who declines to pretend otherwise in front of God.

One detail is worth carrying out of it. The verb in verse 7 usually rendered "you have persuaded me" is the root used for enticing or seducing someone into something. Jeremiah is telling Yahweh, to His face, that he feels he was talked into this under false advertising. And Yahweh's response is to leave the sentence in the book.

The chapter gives permission - not permission to stay bitter, which Jeremiah does not, but permission to bring the whole thing unedited to the only one who sees the heart and the mind and is not startled by what is found there.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 21 - The Way of Life and the Way of Death
chapters.title: The Way of Life and the Way of Death
keyNotes: The setting jumps forward roughly two decades. Babylon is at the walls, Zedekiah is on the throne, and the king who has ignored Jeremiah for years now sends a delegation to ask him to pray (Jeremiah 21:1-2).

The request is precisely worded and utterly hollow: "Perhaps Yahweh will deal with us according to all his wondrous works" - they want another Hezekiah miracle without another Hezekiah (Jeremiah 21:2).
The answer inverts holy war. Yahweh will turn their own weapons back into the middle of the city; the arms raised against Babylon will end up pointed inward (Jeremiah 21:4).
"I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm" takes the exodus vocabulary of deliverance and aims it at Jerusalem (Jeremiah 21:5).
Zedekiah is told his own outcome plainly, years in advance, and the language leaves no room for negotiation: no sparing, no pity, no mercy (Jeremiah 21:6-7).
And then, in the middle of a sealed verdict, a door: "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death." It is the Deuteronomy formula, repurposed for a city under siege (Jeremiah 21:8).
The way of life is humiliating - go out and surrender to the Chaldeans. Survival is offered, but only on terms that require abandoning the city's pride (Jeremiah 21:9).

The word to the palace is not theological but practical: execute justice in the morning, deliver the robbed from the oppressor. The remedy demanded of the house of David is ethical, not ceremonial (Jeremiah 21:11-12).
Jerusalem's confidence is quoted back at her - "Who would come down against us?" - the settled assumption of a people who mistook their geography and their temple for immunity (Jeremiah 21:13).
The chapter closes on the principle underneath the whole book: "I will punish you according to the fruit of your doings." Not arbitrary wrath - harvest (Jeremiah 21:14).

intro: Chronologically this chapter jumps well ahead of the ones on either side of it. Chapters 19 and 20 belong to Jehoiakim's reign; here the Babylonian army is already outside the walls and Zedekiah is the last king Judah will have. The book is arranged by theme rather than by calendar, and the theme here is what happens when a nation finally asks, and asks wrongly.

Look carefully at the request. Zedekiah sends priests to say: perhaps Yahweh will deal with us according to all his wondrous works, that he may withdraw from us. They have Hezekiah in mind - the night the Assyrian camp was struck and Jerusalem woke up delivered without a battle. What they want is that outcome without that posture. Hezekiah tore his clothes and went up into the house of Yahweh himself. Zedekiah sends staff.

And the answer contains the most chilling line in the chapter, because it takes the vocabulary of the exodus and reverses its direction. "With an outstretched hand and with a strong arm" is precisely how Yahweh described bringing Israel out of Egypt. Here the same hand is stretched out and the same arm is strong, and both are aimed at Jerusalem. God will fight against this city, and the fighting men inside it are the ones He is fighting.

So the verdict is settled, which is what makes verse 8 so remarkable. In the middle of an oracle that promises no sparing, no pity and no mercy, Yahweh puts the Deuteronomy choice back on the table: behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. The city is finished. The individual standing in it is not.

But notice what the way of life costs. It is not repentance in the abstract. It is walking out through the gate and surrendering to the besieging army, which every patriot in Jerusalem would have called treason and which is exactly what Jeremiah will later be arrested for recommending. Mercy is offered here in a form that requires the death of national pride before it will save anybody's body.

And the closing line keeps God consistent rather than cruel: I will punish you according to the fruit of your doings. Fruit is not a penalty imposed from outside the situation. It is what grew from what was planted.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 22 - Cedar Palaces and the Signet Plucked Off
chapters.title: Cedar Palaces and the Signet Plucked Off
keyNotes: Jeremiah is sent down to the palace itself - not to summon the king to the temple, but to stand in his house and address him where he governs (Jeremiah 22:1-2).

The requirement laid on the throne is entirely ethical and entirely concrete: justice and righteousness, the robbed delivered, no violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow, no innocent blood (Jeremiah 22:3).
The Davidic promise is presented as conditional in practice. Do this, and kings keep riding through these gates; refuse, and Yahweh swears by Himself that the house becomes a ruin (Jeremiah 22:4-5).
The palace is addressed as a forest - Gilead, the head of Lebanon - because it was panelled in imported cedar. Yahweh promises woodsmen with axes (Jeremiah 22:6-7).
The nations will ask why, and the answer given is not military but covenantal: they abandoned the covenant of Yahweh their God and served other gods (Jeremiah 22:8-9).
Shallum - the king 2 Kings calls Jehoahaz - reigned three months and died in Egypt. Weep for the exiled living rather than the buried dead (Jeremiah 22:10-12).
The woe against Jehoiakim is about labor practices: a wide house with spacious rooms and painted cedar, built by neighbors who were never paid their wages (Jeremiah 22:13-14).

Then the sentence that indicts every religious generation: Josiah did justice and judged the cause of the poor and needy - "wasn't this to know me?" Knowing Yahweh is defined as behavior toward the vulnerable (Jeremiah 22:15-16).
Jehoiakim will be buried with the burial of a donkey, dragged out beyond the gates - no lament, no "Ah, my brother," no royal mourning at all (Jeremiah 22:18-19).

Coniah - Jehoiachin - is called the signet on Yahweh's right hand, the most intimate image of authority available, and is then plucked off it and thrown into a land he was not born in (Jeremiah 22:24-27).
The chapter ends with a triple cry, "O earth, earth, earth," and a verdict recording Coniah as childless: no descendant of his will prosper on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:28-30).

intro: This chapter is a royal audit, and the standard it audits by is not orthodoxy. Yahweh does not ask the kings of Judah about their theology, their attendance at the temple, or their liturgical reforms. He asks what happened to the widow, the orphan, the resident foreigner, and the man whose wages were withheld.

Verse 16 is the hinge, and it repays reading twice. Yahweh describes Josiah - he ate and drank, and did justice and righteousness, and judged the cause of the poor and needy - and then asks, "Wasn't this to know me?" Not: this demonstrated that he knew me. This was knowing Him. The doing and the knowing are presented as the same act, which is a harder claim than it first appears.

Set against that, Jehoiakim's crime is almost mundane. He wanted a better house. Spacious rooms, cut-out windows, cedar panelling, painted vermilion - and he built it with unpaid labour, using his neighbour's service without wages. There is no idol anywhere in his woe. Just a construction project and a payroll he never met.

Then Coniah, and the image Yahweh reaches for is startling in its intimacy. A signet ring is how an ancient king signed his name; it did not leave his hand. Yahweh says that even if Coniah were the signet on His right hand, He would pull him off - and He does.

One thread here becomes important later in the book and later in the Bible. Verse 30 records Coniah as childless, and says no man of his offspring will prosper sitting on David's throne. That reads like the end of the promise. Matthew's genealogy runs Messiah's legal line straight through Jeconiah while Luke traces a different branch of David's house, which is one reason many readers understand the two genealogies as an answer to precisely this verse. And the last four verses of Jeremiah find this same man alive, out of prison, and eating at a king's table.

The standard the chapter sets should be allowed to land where it lands. If knowing God is measured by how the powerless within reach are treated, then a great deal of self-assessment has been done with the wrong instrument.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 23 - The Righteous Branch and the Prophets Who Ran Unsent
chapters.title: The Righteous Branch and the Prophets Who Ran Unsent
keyNotes: The woe falls on the shepherds - the same kings just audited - for scattering the flock and failing to visit them. Yahweh's counter-threat is exact: "I will visit on you" (Jeremiah 23:1-2).
Yahweh then takes the shepherd's job Himself: "I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them," and will set up shepherds who actually feed (Jeremiah 23:3-4).

The promise arrives in the language of horticulture, not politics: a righteous Branch raised up to David, who will reign and deal wisely and execute justice - the very thing the last four kings would not do (Jeremiah 23:5).
His name is the whole gospel in four words: "Yahweh our righteousness." Not a king who enforces righteousness on others, but one who *is* righteousness for the people He rules (Jeremiah 23:6).
As in chapter 16, the coming deliverance will retire the exodus as Israel's defining oath - the new testimony will be the gathering out of the north country (Jeremiah 23:7-8).

Jeremiah's own reaction to the oracles against the prophets is physical: a broken heart, shaking bones, the disorientation of a drunk man - "because of Yahweh, and because of his holy words" (Jeremiah 23:9).
The corruption has reached the sanctuary: "both prophet and priest are profane. Yes, in my house I have found their wickedness" (Jeremiah 23:10-11).
The false prophets' message is diagnosed precisely - they promise peace to those who despise Yahweh and safety to those walking in the stubbornness of their own hearts (Jeremiah 23:16-17).

The test is stated as a question about proximity: who has stood in the council of Yahweh? Had they stood there, they would have turned the people from evil instead of soothing them (Jeremiah 23:18-22).
"Am I a God at hand, and not a God afar off?" answers the theology behind false prophecy - a local, manageable deity who fills a shrine rather than heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:23-24).
The dream-peddlers are contrasted with the faithful: "What is the straw to the wheat?" And the word itself is described as fire and as a hammer that breaks rock (Jeremiah 23:25-29).
The chapter ends by banning a phrase. They had turned "the burden of Yahweh" into a joke, so Yahweh takes the expression away from them entirely (Jeremiah 23:33-40).

intro: Notice how the chapter is built. Yahweh dismantles the shepherds, and then - before saying a word about replacements - says what He Himself will do. I will gather. I will bring them again. I will set up shepherds over them. The failure of leadership is real, and it is not the last word about the flock.

Then comes verse 5, and the metaphor is chosen with care. Judah's royal house has just been described as a cedar forest marked for the axe. Now Yahweh promises a tsemach - a shoot, a sprout, the green thing that comes up out of a stump after the tree has been cut down. The dynasty is going to be felled. Something is going to grow anyway.

And the name stops a reader: Yahweh Tsidkenu, Yahweh Our Righteousness. Every king in the previous chapter was measured by whether he did righteousness. This one is called righteousness - not the enforcer of a standard but the supply of it for the people He governs. The previous chapter asks what a righteous king owes his people; this one answers that the King will be their righteousness.

The rest of the chapter is about how to tell a true word from a comfortable one, and the test in verse 18 is not accuracy or eloquence. It is location. Has this man stood in the council of Yahweh? Because if he had, verse 22 says, he would have come back saying something that turned people from their evil - not something that let them stay where they were. A prophet is identified by his effect, and the effect of a false one is that nothing changes.

There is a wordplay in the closing section that English cannot carry. The word massa means both "oracle" and "burden." The people had begun sneering at Jeremiah in the street - what is the burden of Yahweh today? - and Yahweh answers by confiscating the phrase. You will not use that word any more.

Verse 29 next to verse 17 is the chapter in miniature. One kind of preaching tells people what they wish were true and assures those who despise God that no evil will come to them. The other is fire, and a hammer that breaks rock in pieces. Both feel like ministry from the inside. Only one of them has been anywhere near the council of Yahweh.

verses.4: I will set up shepherds over them, who will feed them. They will no longer be afraid or dismayed, neither will any be lacking,” says Yahweh.
verses.5: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that I will raise to David a righteous Branch, and he will reign as king and deal wisely, and will execute justice and righteousness in the land.

cites.text: “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy, and tell them, even the shepherds, ‘Thus says the Lord Yahweh: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat. You clothe yourself with the wool. You kill the fatlings, but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased. You haven’t healed that which was sick. You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. chapters.heading: CHAPTER 24 - Two Baskets of Figs and a Heart to Know Him
chapters.title: Two Baskets of Figs and a Heart to Know Him
keyNotes: The vision is dated: after Nebuchadnezzar carried off Jeconiah, the princes, the craftsmen and the smiths. This is the deportation of 597 BC, and Jerusalem is still standing (Jeremiah 24:1).
Two baskets sit in front of the temple. One holds figs like the first-ripe - the earliest, sweetest harvest. The other holds figs too rotten to eat (Jeremiah 24:2).
Yahweh asks the prophetic question He asks throughout Scripture - "What do you see, Jeremiah?" - and waits for the man to say it out loud before explaining it (Jeremiah 24:3).
Then the shock. The good figs are the exiles. The people everyone in Jerusalem regarded as the casualties of divine anger are the ones Yahweh regards "for good" (Jeremiah 24:5).
"I will set my eyes on them for good" reverses the language of judgment used earlier in the book, where His eyes were on all their ways for evil (Jeremiah 24:6).

The four verbs of Jeremiah's original call return, and this time only the constructive two are used: "I will build them, and not pull them down. I will plant them, and not pluck them up" (Jeremiah 24:6).
Verse 7 is the theological center: "I will give them a heart to know me." The knowing is not achieved by the exiles - it is given to them, and the returning follows from the gift (Jeremiah 24:7).
The covenant formula appears in full - "They will be my people, and I will be their God" - inside a chapter about deportees rather than temple worshipers (Jeremiah 24:7).

The bad figs are Zedekiah, his princes, the remnant left in Jerusalem, and those who fled to Egypt: everyone still living in the promised land and still congratulating themselves for it (Jeremiah 24:8).
Their sentence is dispersal without purpose - a reproach, a proverb, a taunt, and a curse in every place they are driven, until they are consumed off the land (Jeremiah 24:9-10).

intro: Everything in this chapter depends on knowing who was standing in Jerusalem when it was given.

In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar took the young king Jeconiah, the nobles, and every skilled craftsman and metalworker in the city, and marched them to Babylon. The people left behind drew the obvious conclusion. Those exiles must have been the wicked ones; we are the ones God spared; the temple is still standing and we are still standing in it.

So Yahweh sets two baskets of figs in front of the temple and asks Jeremiah what he sees. The good figs - the first-ripe ones, the kind eaten first because they are the best of the harvest - are the deportees. The rotten figs, too bad to eat, are the congregation still attending services in Jerusalem.

That ought to unsettle anyone who has ever read their own circumstances as a scorecard. Being in the land was not evidence of favour. Being in Babylon was not evidence of rejection. Yahweh says of the exiles, I will set my eyes on them for good - and He says it while they are seven hundred miles from the temple with nothing left of their religion but a memory of it.

Then verse 7, which is the quiet mountain in this chapter: I will give them a heart to know me. Not I will command them to know me. Not I will wait for them to decide to know me. I will give them the organ with which knowing happens. And notice the order - the heart is given first, and their returning to Him with their whole heart follows from it. Grace is upstream of repentance here, and Jeremiah says so seven chapters before he says it again in the new covenant passage.
The losses that looked like judgement may be the furnace in which a heart to know Him is formed. The people with everything still intact were the ones in trouble.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 25 - Twenty-Three Years, Seventy Years, and the Cup No Nation Refuses
chapters.title: Twenty-Three Years, Seventy Years, and the Cup No Nation Refuses
keyNotes: The chapter is dated to Jehoiakim's fourth year - the same year Nebuchadnezzar took the throne. Two clocks start together, and one of them is running out (Jeremiah 25:1-2).

Jeremiah counts his own ministry: twenty-three years of speaking, "rising up early and speaking; but you have not listened." The idiom pictures a man who gets up before dawn to try again (Jeremiah 25:3).
He was not alone. Yahweh sent "all his servants the prophets," and the response to every one of them was the same silence (Jeremiah 25:4).
The message they all carried was startlingly modest: turn from evil, don't chase other gods, and you may stay in the land. The offer was never complicated (Jeremiah 25:5-6).
Nebuchadnezzar is called "my servant" - a pagan emperor given the same title as Moses and David, because sovereignty is not limited to those who acknowledge it (Jeremiah 25:9).
The judgment is described by what will go missing: mirth, gladness, bridegroom, bride, the sound of millstones, the light of a lamp. Ordinary domestic noise, and then nothing (Jeremiah 25:10).
Then comes the number that changes everything. Seventy years - the first time this catastrophe is given a boundary. Exile is announced with an expiry date attached (Jeremiah 25:11).
And Babylon is not exempt. When the seventy years are done, the instrument of judgment is judged in turn, for exactly the same reason: iniquity (Jeremiah 25:12-14).

Jeremiah is handed the cup of the wine of wrath and told to make the nations drink. The vision moves from Jerusalem outward through Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, Arabia, Elam, Media, and finally Sheshach - a cipher for Babylon itself (Jeremiah 25:15-26).
The most sobering line in the chapter is the order of service: "I begin to work evil at the city which is called by my name." Judgment starts at the household of God (Jeremiah 25:29).
The imagery turns cosmic - Yahweh roaring from His holy habitation, treading grapes, entering into judgment with all flesh, a great storm rising from the ends of the earth (Jeremiah 25:30-33).
The chapter closes on the shepherds again: wail, wallow in dust, no way to flee, no escape - the leaders who lost the flock are the last ones offered cover (Jeremiah 25:34-38).

intro: Twenty-three years. That is what verse 3 puts on the table before anything else happens - not a doctrine but an accounting. Jeremiah has been preaching since the thirteenth year of Josiah, through a reformation and a relapse and three kings, and the summary of the whole period fits in five words: you have not listened.

The Hebrew idiom behind "rising up early and speaking" is worth slowing down for. It pictures someone who gets up before dawn, day after day, hoping this is the morning it lands. Yahweh uses it of Himself twice in this chapter, once of His own speaking and once of the prophets He kept sending. That is not the vocabulary of a God who lost patience quickly.

Then verse 11 does something the book has not done before. It puts a number on the disaster. Seventy years - not forever, seventy. Chronicles later reads that figure as the land finally collecting the sabbath rests it had been denied, and Daniel is found reading this very verse in exile and beginning to pray because he realised the clock was almost run out. A boundary is a mercy. It means the thing has an end, and that God set the end Himself.

And then the cup. Jeremiah is handed it and told to make the nations drink, and the list runs outward in widening rings from Jerusalem - Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Tyre, Arabia, Elam, Media - and finishes with Sheshach, an old scribal cipher in which the letters of Babel are written in reverse. Even the hand holding the rod drinks, and it drinks last.

But notice where the pouring starts. Verse 29: I begin to work evil at the city which is called by my name. Not the pagans first, with the covenant people taking whatever wrath is left over. His own house, first. Peter says the same thing seven centuries later in almost the same words.

Both halves of the chapter have to be held together. The God who sets a seventy-year limit on His own people's discipline is the God who hands the cup to every kingdom on earth. Neither the mercy nor the severity is a mood. Both are exact.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 26 - The Temple Sermon on Trial
chapters.title: The Temple Sermon on Trial
keyNotes: This is the same sermon as chapter 7, told from the outside: chapter 7 gives the content, chapter 26 gives the consequences (Jeremiah 26:1-2).
The commissioning includes a warning that preachers have quoted ever since: "Don't omit a word." The temptation to soften was anticipated (Jeremiah 26:2).
The purpose clause is pure mercy: "It may be they will listen... that I may relent." The sermon is delivered in hope of not having to be fulfilled (Jeremiah 26:3).
The threat that detonates the chapter is one word: Shiloh. Yahweh had let His own sanctuary there be destroyed once already, and everyone in the courtyard knew it (Jeremiah 26:6).
The reaction is immediate and unanimous - priests, prophets, and all the people seize him: "You shall surely die!" The clergy lead the mob (Jeremiah 26:7-9).
The civil authorities arrive and convene a court in the entry of the New Gate. Jeremiah's life is spared, in part, by the separation of powers (Jeremiah 26:10-11).
His defense is not a legal maneuver. He repeats the sermon, renews the offer of repentance, and then says, "as for me, behold, I am in your hand" (Jeremiah 26:12-14).
The one warning he adds is about them, not him: kill me and you bring innocent blood on yourselves and on this city (Jeremiah 26:15).
The verdict turns on a precedent from a hundred years earlier: Micah said Zion would be plowed as a field, and Hezekiah repented instead of executing him (Jeremiah 26:16-19).
Then the chapter tells a second story with the opposite ending. Uriah preached the same message, fled to Egypt in fear, was extradited, and was killed by Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20-23).
Jeremiah lives because one man stood in the gap - "the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah." Providence often has a name and an address (Jeremiah 26:24).

intro: The temple sermon was given seven chapters ago. This chapter is what it cost.

The instruction beforehand should make anyone who has ever had to say a hard thing pause: don't omit a word. Yahweh knows exactly which sentence Jeremiah will be tempted to leave out - the one about Shiloh - and forbids the omission in advance.

Shiloh was the pressure point. It was where the tabernacle stood for something like three centuries, and it was destroyed, and archaeologists have found the burn layer. Everyone in that courtyard knew the story and had quietly concluded it could not happen twice, because this time there was a temple and not a tent. Jeremiah says the quiet part out loud, and the priests and prophets move to kill him within the hour.

Then watch the trial, because two things save his life and neither of them is a miracle. The first is a handful of old men who remember their own history: Micah of Moresheth said this same thing about Zion a century earlier, and Hezekiah's response was repentance rather than execution. Scripture cited from memory, in a courtroom, by laymen, keeps a prophet alive.

The second is Ahikam, who gets one verse and no speech. He was a son of Shaphan, from the scribal family that had found the scroll in Josiah's day, and his hand was with Jeremiah so that the crowd did not get him. His son Gedaliah will protect Jeremiah again after the city falls, and will be murdered for his trouble.

But the chapter refuses to be tidy. Uriah the son of Shemaiah preached the same message, fled to Egypt, was extradited by the king, and was killed and thrown into a commoner's grave. Same word, same courage, different ending. Faithfulness is not a guarantee of survival, and this book will not pretend otherwise.

What Jeremiah himself says when his life is in the balance is worth noticing. Not a defence and not a retraction. As for me, behold, I am in your hand; do with me what is good and right in your eyes. And then one more warning, delivered on behalf of the people about to decide his fate.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 27 - The Yoke on the Prophet's Own Neck
chapters.title: The Yoke on the Prophet's Own Neck
keyNotes: Jeremiah is told to make a yoke - bonds and bars, the working harness of an ox - and wear it himself. He does not describe submission; he carries it (Jeremiah 27:2).
The audience is international. Envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon are in Jerusalem plotting a coalition, and Jeremiah is to send each of them home with a message (Jeremiah 27:3).
The theological ground is laid first: "I have made the earth... I give it to whom it seems right to me." Sovereignty over the nations is grounded in creation, not in covenant (Jeremiah 27:5).
Nebuchadnezzar is again called "my servant," and the grant is explicitly temporary - through his son and his son's son, and then Babylon's own turn comes (Jeremiah 27:6-7).
The terms are blunt: the nation that puts its neck under the yoke stays on its land and farms it. The nation that refuses is consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence (Jeremiah 27:8-11).
The list of voices to ignore is long and modern: prophets, diviners, dreamers, soothsayers, sorcerers - a whole industry unified by telling people what they wanted (Jeremiah 27:9-10).
To Zedekiah personally the message is reduced to five words of ordinary imperative: bring your neck under, and live (Jeremiah 27:12).
To the priests the issue is the temple vessels. The comfortable prophecy circulating was that the articles taken in 597 would be back shortly, and it was a lie (Jeremiah 27:16).
Jeremiah proposes a test that costs nothing and exposes everything: if they are really prophets, let them intercede - and see whether the rest of the vessels stay (Jeremiah 27:18).
The chapter ends where every hard word in this book eventually ends. The vessels go to Babylon - and then, "until the day that I visit them," they come home (Jeremiah 27:22).

intro: There is a particular humiliation in this chapter that is easy to read past. Jeremiah does not preach about submission. He builds a yoke - the wooden bars and leather straps that go on an ox - and wears it, in public, in a capital city full of foreign envoys, for as long as it takes.

And what he tells them is politically indefensible. There is a coalition forming in Jerusalem: envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, meeting with Zedekiah about exactly the kind of alliance any competent government would pursue. Jeremiah walks into it wearing a harness and tells them all to go home and submit.

Notice how he grounds it. Not with "because Judah has sinned" - these are foreign kings and that argument has no purchase on them. He goes back further, to creation: I have made the earth, the men and the animals on it, by my great power and my outstretched arm, and I give it to whom it seems right to me. The claim is not covenantal. It is proprietary.

Then he gives Babylon an expiry date in the same breath in which he gives it an empire. Nebuchadnezzar, his son, and his son's son - and then many nations and great kings will make him their servant. Three generations, and the historical record lands close to exactly there. Submission is commanded, and it is never presented as permanent.

The sharpest moment is verse 18, and it is worth remembering whenever anyone claims to speak for God. Jeremiah proposes a test: if these men are really prophets, let them pray. Not preach - pray. Let them stand between Yahweh and the temple vessels that are still in Jerusalem and ask that the vessels not go to Babylon. He is measuring the prophetic office by intercession rather than by prediction, and the false prophets have nothing to offer, because men whose business is telling people what they want have never learned to stand in a gap.

And notice how the chapter ends. Not with the yoke. With the vessels coming back - until the day that I visit them, then I will bring them up and restore them to this place. Even a chapter about wearing a harness closes with a homecoming.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 28 - Hananiah, the Broken Bar, and the Yoke of Iron
chapters.title: Hananiah, the Broken Bar, and the Yoke of Iron
keyNotes: Hananiah is not an outsider. He is called "the prophet," he speaks in Yahweh's house, before the priests and all the people, and he opens with the proper formula: "Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says" (Jeremiah 28:1-2).
His message is everything a frightened nation wants: the yoke is already broken, the vessels come back, the king comes back, and all of it inside two years (Jeremiah 28:2-4).
Jeremiah's first response is the most disarming sentence in the chapter: "Amen! May Yahweh do so." He genuinely wishes his opponent were right (Jeremiah 28:6).
Then he lays down the historical test. The prophets before them both prophesied war, evil, and pestilence - the burden of proof sits differently on a man promising peace (Jeremiah 28:7-8).
The criterion he gives is not a feeling and not a credential: when the word of the prophet happens, then the prophet will be known. Verification is deferred to fulfillment (Jeremiah 28:9).
Hananiah answers theology with theater. He takes the bar off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it in front of everyone - a counter-sign, performed on another man's body (Jeremiah 28:10-11).
Jeremiah does not retaliate. "Then the prophet Jeremiah went his way." He leaves the room without a word, and waits for a word (Jeremiah 28:11).
The word comes, and it is devastating in its economy: you have broken bars of wood, and made in their place bars of iron (Jeremiah 28:13).
The false comfort did not prevent the yoke. It hardened it. Resistance to a discipline does not cancel the discipline; it changes what the discipline is made of (Jeremiah 28:14).
The charge against Hananiah is specific and it is pastoral: "you make this people trust in a lie." The damage named is not doctrinal error but misplaced trust (Jeremiah 28:15).
The sentence is given with a date, and verse 17 records it landing two months later - the shortest and grimmest fulfillment notice in the book (Jeremiah 28:16-17).

intro: The thing to understand about Hananiah is that nothing about him looked wrong.

He was a prophet by title. He spoke in the house of Yahweh, in front of the priests, with the whole congregation present. He used the correct formula - Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says. His message was patriotic, hopeful and specific: within two full years the vessels and the exiles will be back. And he was, as far as anyone can tell from the text, sincere.

That is what makes the chapter uncomfortable. There was no external marker separating him from Jeremiah. Same venue, same vocabulary, same God invoked, opposite messages, and no way for a listener in that courtyard to tell them apart by inspection.

Watch what Jeremiah does with that. He does not sneer. His first word is Amen, and he means it - may Yahweh do so, may Yahweh perform your words. A man who had been beaten, jailed and boycotted for twenty years still wanted the good news to be true.

Then he offers the only test available, and it is a hard one: wait. The prophet who prophesies peace is known when the word comes to pass. There is no shortcut, no credential, no anointing that substitutes for time. That test is unsatisfying precisely because it cannot be gamed.

And Hananiah cannot wait. He takes the yoke off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it - a counter-sign performed on somebody else's body, which is its own kind of tell. Jeremiah says nothing at all and walks away. He has no word yet, so he does not manufacture one; the silence between verse 11 and verse 12 is a discipline most people have never practised.

The word, when it comes, is the sentence to carry out of the chapter: you have broken bars of wood, and you have made in their place bars of iron. The comfortable message did not remove the yoke. It upgraded it.
The danger of a false word is almost never that it sounds false. It is that it sounds like exactly what was hoped for, delivered by somebody carrying every credential anyone knows how to check.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 29 - The Letter to Babylon
chapters.title: The Letter to Babylon
keyNotes: This is a real letter, carried by named couriers on a diplomatic mission - Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, traveling to Babylon on Zedekiah's business (Jeremiah 29:1-3).
The recipients are the 597 deportees: elders, priests, prophets, and the people taken with Jeconiah - the same group chapter 24 called the good figs (Jeremiah 29:1-2).
The instructions are almost aggressively ordinary. Build houses. Live in them. Plant gardens. Eat what grows. Marry, and let your children marry (Jeremiah 29:5-6).
"Multiply there, and don't be diminished" is a deliberate echo of Genesis. Exile is not a suspension of the creation mandate (Jeremiah 29:6).
Then the astonishing command: seek the peace of the city that took you captive, and pray for it - because your welfare is bound up in its welfare (Jeremiah 29:7).
The warning that follows is the reason the letter was needed. Prophets in Babylon were promising a quick return, and people were living out of suitcases because of it (Jeremiah 29:8-9).
The timeline is restated: seventy years for Babylon, and then "I will visit you and perform my good word toward you." The promise has a schedule (Jeremiah 29:10).
Verse 11 is spoken to people who will die in Babylon. "Thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future" is not a promise of comfort now, but of a future secured (Jeremiah 29:11).
The conditions that follow are relational, not transactional: call on me, pray, seek me - and the qualifier is total, "when you search for me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:12-13).
Those still in Jerusalem, congratulating themselves on not having been deported, are told they are the rotten figs - sword, famine, pestilence (Jeremiah 29:15-19).
Two named false prophets in Babylon, Ahab and Zedekiah, are exposed for adultery and lying in Yahweh's name, and Yahweh says simply: "I am he who knows, and am witness" (Jeremiah 29:21-23).

Shemaiah writes his own letter demanding Jeremiah be put in the stocks - and is answered with a sentence that stings more than punishment: he will not see the good I will do for my people (Jeremiah 29:24-32).

intro: Verse 11 has been printed on more graduation cards than any other sentence in this book, and almost none of them mention who was holding the letter.

The recipients had watched their city looted. They had walked to Babylon in a column. Their king was in a foreign prison. Most of the people who first read those words would die without seeing Jerusalem again, because seventy years is longer than a life was in the ancient world. That is the audience for "thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future."

Which does not make the promise smaller. It makes it sturdier. It is not an assurance that this year will go well. It is an assurance that the trajectory is not abandonment, spoken to people with every reason available to believe otherwise.

And look at what He actually asks of them in the meantime. Build houses and live in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit. Marry, have sons and daughters, take wives for your sons - and multiply there, which is the Genesis word, used of the creation mandate and now applied to a prison camp. Not: hold on, keep your bags packed, this is temporary. Sink roots into the soil of the place that took everything.

Then verse 7, which is among the most remarkable instructions in the Old Testament: seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it. Pray for Babylon. Not against it - for it. Because in its peace you will have peace.

There is a pastoral reason underneath all of it, and the chapter states it plainly a few verses later. Prophets in Babylon were promising an imminent return, and people were declining to plant anything because they expected to leave. False hope had made an entire community unable to live. Sometimes the kindest word God gives is the one that ends the waiting and lets a person start their life.

And notice the order in verses 12 and 13. Call, pray, seek - and then you shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart. The finding is promised outright. The condition is that we stop looking for Him with only part of ourselves.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 30 - Jacob's Trouble and the Wound That Gets Healed
chapters.title: Jacob's Trouble and the Wound That Gets Healed
keyNotes: Chapters 30 through 33 are usually called the Book of Consolation, and this one opens with a publishing order: write all the words I have spoken to you in a book (Jeremiah 30:1-2).
The scope is deliberately wide - "my people Israel and Judah." The northern kingdom, gone for a century, is included in the restoration (Jeremiah 30:3-4).
The chapter does not skip the pain to get to the promise. It opens with trembling, fear, and men doubled over with their hands on their waists like women in labor (Jeremiah 30:5-6).
"It is even the time of Jacob's trouble; but he will be saved out of it." Both halves of that verse matter, and the second half is the point (Jeremiah 30:7).
The yoke that dominated chapters 27 and 28 is finally broken - not by a Hananiah snapping a bar, but by Yahweh in His own appointed day (Jeremiah 30:8).
The restored people will serve "Yahweh their God, and David their king, whom I will raise up to them" - written four centuries after David died (Jeremiah 30:9).
The discipline is bounded on both sides: a full end of the nations, but not of you; correction in measure, and yet not left unpunished (Jeremiah 30:10-11).
Then the diagnosis returns in its bluntest form - incurable hurt, a grievous wound, no one to plead the cause, no healing medicines, and lovers who have forgotten (Jeremiah 30:12-14).
Yahweh takes responsibility for the wound without apologizing for it: "I have wounded you with the wound of an enemy" - and the reason given is the greatness of their iniquity (Jeremiah 30:14-15).
And then the turn, on one word: "Therefore." Therefore the devourers are devoured, the plunderers become plunder, and the incurable wound is healed by the One who gave it (Jeremiah 30:16-17).
The reason given for the healing is almost tender: "because they have called you an outcast, saying, It is Zion, whom no man seeks after." He acts because no one else would (Jeremiah 30:17).
The restoration is domestic and specific - tents, dwelling places, a city rebuilt on its own ruin-heap, thanksgiving, laughter, children, a congregation established (Jeremiah 30:18-20).
Verse 21 asks a question the whole Bible is answering: their ruler will come from among them and approach Yahweh - "for who is he who has had boldness to approach to me?" (Jeremiah 30:21).

intro: Twenty-nine chapters of demolition, and then a publishing order: write all the words that I have spoken to you in a book. Something is about to be said that Yahweh wants preserved in permanent form.

What follows in chapters 30 through 33 is the most sustained comfort in Jeremiah, and this chapter sets the pattern for it. It does not reach the comfort by going around the pain. It goes straight through the middle.

Verse 6 is a strange and vivid image - men doubled over with their hands on their loins like a woman in labour, every face gone pale. It is the prophet reaching for the only comparison violent enough to carry it. And labour is not an accidental metaphor. It is agony that produces something.

"The time of Jacob's trouble" has become a technical phrase in a good deal of prophetic teaching, and readers disagree about how far forward it reaches. What nobody can miss is the clause fastened to it: but he will be saved out of it. The trouble is named and bounded in the same breath.

Then comes the passage that makes this chapter unforgettable. Verses 12 through 15 are as bleak as anything in the book - your hurt is incurable, your wound grievous, there is no one to plead your cause, you have no healing medicines, all your lovers have forgotten you - and Yahweh takes responsibility for the wound. I have wounded you. I struck you as an enemy would.

And then verse 16 begins with one word: therefore. Not nevertheless. Not but. Therefore. Because the wound is incurable and nobody else will bind it, therefore I will restore health to you and heal you of your wounds. The hopelessness of the case is the reason He acts, rather than the obstacle to His acting.
His stated motive is worth carrying: because they have called you an outcast, saying, "It is Zion, whom no man seeks after." He moves toward the one nobody was coming for.

And verse 21 is left deliberately unanswered. "Who is he who has had boldness to approach to me?" Jeremiah does not name him. He says only that the ruler will come from among their own people, and that Yahweh Himself will cause him to draw near - which is a considerable thing to say about a man's ability to stand in that particular place.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 31 - Everlasting Love and the New Covenant
chapters.title: Everlasting Love and the New Covenant
keyNotes: The chapter opens with the covenant formula stretched to its widest reach - not Judah only, but "all the families of Israel," including the northern tribes gone for a century (Jeremiah 31:1).
"I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness." The drawing is the consequence of the loving, not its reward (Jeremiah 31:3).
The return is pictured as a party, not a procession - tambourines, dancing, vineyards planted on the mountains of Samaria by people who will live to eat the fruit (Jeremiah 31:4-5).
The gathered company is deliberately unimpressive: the blind, the lame, the pregnant, the woman in labor. Nobody is left behind for slowing the column down (Jeremiah 31:8).
"He who scattered Israel will gather him." The same hand does both, which is why the exile was never a sign that He had lost track of them (Jeremiah 31:10).
Rachel is heard weeping in Ramah - the staging town for deportation - and is told to stop, because "there is hope for your latter end" (Jeremiah 31:15-17).
Ephraim's repentance is quoted back with a prayer inside it: "Turn me, and I will be turned." Even the turning is asked for as a gift (Jeremiah 31:18).
Yahweh's answer is the most emotional line in the book: "my heart yearns for him. I will surely have mercy on him." The Hebrew is visceral, the language of a parent's insides (Jeremiah 31:20).
The four demolition verbs of chapter 1 are answered at last - He watched to pluck up and break down; now He watches to build and to plant (Jeremiah 31:28).
A proverb is formally retired. No more "the fathers have eaten sour grapes" - each person will die for his own iniquity, and the excuse of inherited fate goes with it (Jeremiah 31:29-30).
Then the new covenant: not like the one they broke, but Torah written on the inward parts, a knowledge of Yahweh needing no intermediary, and sin remembered no more (Jeremiah 31:31-34).
The guarantee is cosmological. Israel's continuance is pinned to the fixed order of sun, moon, and sea - if those fail, then and only then does the promise fail (Jeremiah 31:35-37).
The chapter ends by taking the valley of dead bodies and ashes - the Hinnom of chapter 19 - and declaring it holy to Yahweh, never to be plucked up again (Jeremiah 31:38-40).

intro: Start with verse 3, because everything else in this chapter runs downhill from it. "I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness." Read the logic carefully. He did not draw them and then decide to love them. The love came first, and the drawing is what the love does.

That order matters enormously by the time the chapter reaches verse 18, where Ephraim prays the strangest and most honest prayer in the book: turn me, and I will be turned. He does not say I will turn. He asks to be turned. He has apparently tried, and discovered that repentance is something that has to be done to him before he can do it.

And the reply in verse 20 is worth reading aloud. The Hebrew behind "my heart yearns for him" refers to the inward parts - the churn in the gut when someone you love is in trouble - and it is built on the same root as the word for a womb. This is not a formal pardon issued from a bench. It is a father who cannot help himself.

The chapter is also where Rachel appears, weeping in Ramah for children who are not there. Ramah was the staging camp where deportees were sorted before the march to Babylon, which is why she is placed there, and Matthew will reach for the verse again at Bethlehem. Yahweh's answer to her is one of the gentlest sentences in the prophets: refrain your voice from weeping, for your work will be rewarded, and there is hope for your latter end.

Then comes verse 31 and the phrase that gives the second half of the Bible its name - a new covenant, berit hadashah, which the Greek renders kaine diatheke. Notice what is new about it and what is not. The content is not replaced: I will put my law in their inward parts and write it in their heart. It is the same Torah. What changes is the location. It moves from tablets to tissue, from an external standard to an internal instinct.

And the final clause is what makes it good news rather than merely a better delivery system: I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. Hebrews quotes these four verses twice, at greater length than any other Old Testament passage appears in the New, and both times the writer lands on that line.

Hold the last verse of the chapter next to chapter 19. The valley of the dead bodies and of the ashes is Hinnom - the place where children were burned, the place Yahweh renamed the Valley of Slaughter. Here He says it will be holy to Yahweh, and never plucked up or thrown down again. If He will do that with that valley, there is nothing in anyone's history He cannot consecrate.

verses.1: “At that time,” says Yahweh, “I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be my people.”
verses.2: Yahweh says, “The people who survive the sword found favor in the wilderness; even Israel, when I went to cause him to rest.”
verses.3: Yahweh appeared of old to me, saying, “Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness.
verses.4: I will build you again, and you will be built, O virgin of Israel. You will again be adorned with your tambourines, and will go out in the dances of those who make merry.
verses.5: Again you will plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria. The planters will plant, and will enjoy its fruit.
verses.6: For there will be a day that the watchmen on the hills of Ephraim cry, ‘Arise, and let us go up to Zion to Yahweh our God.’”
verses.7: For Yahweh says, “Sing with gladness for Jacob, and shout for the chief of the nations. Publish, praise, and say, ‘Yahweh, save your people, the remnant of Israel!’
verses.8: Behold, I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the uttermost parts of the earth, along with the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her who travails with child together. They will return as a great company.
verses.9: They will come with weeping. I will lead them with petitions. I will cause them to walk by rivers of waters, in a straight way in which they won’t stumble; for I am a father to Israel. Ephraim is my firstborn.
verses.10: “Hear Yahweh’s word, you nations, and declare it in the distant islands. Say, ‘He who scattered Israel will gather him, and keep him, as a shepherd does his flock.’
verses.11: For Yahweh has ransomed Jacob, and redeemed him from the hand of him who was stronger than he.
verses.12: They will come and sing in the height of Zion, and will flow to the goodness of Yahweh, to the grain, to the new wine, to the oil, and to the young of the flock and of the herd. Their soul will be as a watered garden. They will not sorrow any more at all.
verses.13: Then the virgin will rejoice in the dance; the young men and the old together; for I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow.
verses.14: I will satiate the soul of the priests with fatness, and my people will be satisfied with my goodness,” says Yahweh.
verses.15: Yahweh says: “A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children. She refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more.”
verses.16: Yahweh says: “Refrain your voice from weeping, and your eyes from tears; for your work will be rewarded,” says Yahweh. “They will come again from the land of the enemy.
verses.17: There is hope for your latter end,” says Yahweh. “Your children will come again to their own territory.
verses.18: “I have surely heard Ephraim grieving thus, ‘You have chastised me, and I was chastised, as an untrained calf. Turn me, and I will be turned; for you are Yahweh my God.
verses.19: Surely after that I was turned. I repented. After that I was instructed. I struck my thigh. I was ashamed, yes, even confounded, because I bore the reproach of my youth.’
verses.20: Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he a darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I still earnestly remember him. therefore my heart yearns for him. I will surely have mercy on him,” says Yahweh.
verses.21: “Set up road signs. Make guideposts. Set your heart toward the highway, even the way by which you went. Turn again, virgin of Israel. Turn again to these your cities.
verses.22: How long will you go here and there, you backsliding daughter? For Yahweh has created a new thing in the earth: a woman will encompass a man.”
verses.23: Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Yet again they will use this speech in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I reverse their captivity: ‘Yahweh bless you, habitation of righteousness, mountain of holiness.’
verses.24: Judah and all its cities will dwell therein together, the farmers, and those who go about with flocks.
verses.25: For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.”
verses.26: On this I awakened, and saw; and my sleep was sweet to me.
verses.27: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and with the seed of animal.
verses.28: It will happen that, like as I have watched over them to pluck up and to break down and to overthrow and to destroy and to afflict, so will I watch over them to build and to plant,” says Yahweh.
verses.29: “In those days they will say no more, “‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.’
verses.30: But everyone will die for his own iniquity. Every man who eats the sour grapes, his teeth will be set on edge.
verses.31: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
verses.32: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them,” says Yahweh.
verses.33: “But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,” says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
verses.34: They will no longer each teach his neighbor, and every man teach his brother, saying, ‘Know Yahweh;’ for they will all know me, from their least to their greatest,” says Yahweh: “for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.”
verses.35: Yahweh, who gives the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, who stirs up the sea, so that its waves roar; Yahweh of Armies is his name, says:
verses.36: “If these ordinances depart from before me,” says Yahweh, “then the offspring of Israel also will cease from being a nation before me forever.”
verses.37: Yahweh says: “If heaven above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth searched out beneath, then I will also cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done,” says Yahweh.
verses.38: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the city will be built to Yahweh from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner.
verses.39: The measuring line will go out further straight onward to the hill Gareb, and will turn toward Goah.
verses.40: The whole valley of the dead bodies and of the ashes, and all the fields to the brook Kidron, to the corner of the horse gate toward the east, will be holy to Yahweh. It will not be plucked up or thrown down any more forever.”

I drew them with cords of a man, with ties of love; and I was to them like those who lift up the yoke on their necks; and I bent down to him and I fed him.

cites.text: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from God’s love, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.

3.why: nothing able to separate us from the love of God, having loved His own to the end

cites.text: As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep. I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day.
and not for the nation only, but that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.

10.why: the shepherd seeking out scattered sheep, gathering into one the children of God

cites.text: who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works.

knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things, with silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ;

cites.text: Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked by the wise men, was exceedingly angry, and sent out, and killed all the male children who were in Bethlehem and in all the surrounding countryside, from two years old and under, according to the exact time which he had learned from the wise men. Then that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled, saying, “A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children; she wouldn’t be comforted, because they are no more.”
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away.”

15.why: Rachel's weeping heard again at Bethlehem, and every tear finally wiped away

cites.text: Turn us to yourself, Yahweh, and we will be turned. Renew our days as of old.
Turn us again, God. Cause your face to shine, and we will be saved.

18.why: turn us to yourself and we shall be turned - repentance asked for as a gift, not achieved

cites.text: “How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I make you like Zeboiim? My heart is turned within me, my compassion is aroused.

Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul who sins, he shall die.
The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers. Every man shall be put to death for his own sin.

29.why: the same proverb answered by Ezekiel, and the Torah's rule that each dies for his own sin

Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.’ These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel.”

31.why: the Sinai covenant sealed in blood, and the terms this new one is measured against

For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, since a death has occurred for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first covenant, that those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.

31.why: this cup is the new covenant in my blood, and the Mediator of a better one

cites.text: being revealed that you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh.

I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them.

33.why: written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts, by the Spirit given within
