intro: This is the last sermon of Jeremiah's life that scripture records, and it is the only one where the congregation answers back out loud. Nowhere else in the prophets does a whole assembly stand up and reply. What they say is no.

Read verse 17 slowly, because it is one of the most honest arguments any idolater ever made and it is built entirely out of data. When we burned incense to the queen of the sky and poured out drink offerings to her, we had plenty of food, we were well, and we saw no evil. Since we stopped, we have lacked everything and been consumed by sword and famine. That is not superstition. That is a chart. They lived through Josiah's reform and then through the collapse, and they drew the obvious line between the two.

And they got it exactly backwards. The reform was the last mercy before a judgement that generations had already earned; the disasters that followed were the bill arriving, not the penalty for cleaning house. But it is not hard to see how it looked from inside. Correlation is a terrible pastor, and an entire nation ordered its worship around it.

The queen of the sky is Ishtar, or Astarte, and the detail worth noticing is how homely her cult was. Cakes pressed in a mould with her face on them. Drink poured out at the door. This was not a state religion imposed from a palace; it was a family practice, run out of the kitchen, taught by mothers to daughters. Chapter 7 already showed the whole household at it - children gathering wood, fathers lighting the fire, women kneading the dough. The most durable idolatry is almost always the domestic kind.

The women's reply in verse 19 deserves respect even in its defiance, because it is true. Did we make her cakes and pour out drink offerings to her without our husbands? No, they did not. The men had known, and approved, and eaten. When Jeremiah answers he does not accept the division at all - he addresses the men, the women, and all the people together. There is no innocent party in the room.

Then comes verse 25, and God stops arguing. "Establish then your vows, and perform your vows." Go ahead. Do it. It is the sound of a door being deliberately left open, and it is far more frightening than any threat in the chapter. There is a judgement that consists simply of being permitted.

And the sentence in verse 26 has no parallel anywhere: my name will no more be named in the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt. They had used the phrase "as the Lord Yahweh lives" as a formality while serving another god - a signature on documents, a habit of speech. So the signature is revoked. The judgement is not that He shouts at them. It is that the sound of His name goes out of their mouths.

Listen for the question in verse 28, because it is the question the entire book has been asking: they will know whose word will stand, mine or theirs. Everything else - the kings, the sieges, the false prophets, the burned scroll, the cistern - has been a long argument about that one sentence. It is still the only question that matters about anything anyone is currently sure of.

verses.1: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews who lived in the land of Egypt, who lived at Migdol, and at Tahpanhes, and at Memphis, and in the country of Pathros, saying,
verses.2: “Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘You have seen all the evil that I have brought on Jerusalem, and on all the cities of Judah. Behold, today they are a desolation, and no man dwells in them,
verses.3: because of their wickedness which they have committed to provoke me to anger, in that they went to burn incense, to serve other gods that they didn’t know, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.
verses.4: However I sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them, saying, “Oh, don’t do this abominable thing that I hate.”
verses.5: But they didn’t listen and didn’t incline their ear. They didn’t turn from their wickedness, to stop burning incense to other gods.
verses.6: Therefore my wrath and my anger was poured out, and was kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem; and they are wasted and desolate, as it is today.’
verses.7: “Therefore now Yahweh, the God of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Why do you commit great evil against your own souls, to cut off from yourselves man and woman, infant and nursing child out of the middle of Judah, to leave yourselves no one remaining;
verses.8: in that you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, burning incense to other gods in the land of Egypt, where you have gone to live; that you may be cut off, and that you may be a curse and a reproach among all the nations of the earth?
verses.9: Have you forgotten the wickedness of your fathers, and the wickedness of the kings of Judah, and the wickedness of their wives, and your own wickedness, and the wickedness of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
verses.10: They are not humbled even to this day, neither have they feared, nor walked in my law, nor in my statutes, that I set before you and before your fathers.’
verses.11: “Therefore Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I will set my face against you for evil, even to cut off all Judah.
verses.12: I will take the remnant of Judah, that have set their faces to go into the land of Egypt to live there, and they will all be consumed. They will fall in the land of Egypt. They will be consumed by the sword and by the famine. They will die, from the least even to the greatest, by the sword and by the famine. They will be an object of horror, an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach.
verses.13: For I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence;
verses.14: so that none of the remnant of Judah, who have gone into the land of Egypt to live there, will escape or be left to return into the land of Judah, to which they have a desire to return to dwell there; for no one will return except those who will escape.’”
verses.15: Then all the men who knew that their wives burned incense to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, even all the people who lived in the land of Egypt, in Pathros, answered Jeremiah, saying,
verses.16: “As for the word that you have spoken to us in Yahweh’s name, we will not listen to you.
verses.17: But we will certainly perform every word that has gone out of our mouth, to burn incense to the queen of the sky, and to pour out drink offerings to her, as we have done, we and our fathers, our kings and our princes, in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem; for then had we plenty of food, and were well, and saw no evil.
verses.18: But since we stopped burning incense to the queen of the sky, and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked all things, and have been consumed by the sword and by the famine.
verses.19: “When we burned incense to the queen of the sky, and poured out drink offerings to her, did we make her cakes to worship her, and pour out drink offerings to her, without our husbands?”
verses.20: Then Jeremiah said to all the people, to the men, and to the women, even to all the people who had given him an answer, saying,
verses.21: “The incense that you burned in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your princes, and the people of the land, didn’t Yahweh remember them, and didn’t it come into his mind?
verses.22: Thus Yahweh could no longer bear it, because of the evil of your doings, and because of the abominations which you have committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation, and an astonishment, and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is today.
verses.23: Because you have burned incense, and because you have sinned against Yahweh, and have not obeyed Yahweh’s voice, nor walked in his law, nor in his statutes, nor in his testimonies; therefore this evil has happened to you, as it is today.”
verses.24: Moreover Jeremiah said to all the people, including all the women, “Hear Yahweh’s word, all Judah who are in the land of Egypt!
verses.25: Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says, ‘You and your wives have both spoken with your mouths, and with your hands have fulfilled it, saying, “We will surely perform our vows that we have vowed, to burn incense to the queen of the sky, and to pour out drink offerings to her.” “‘Establish then your vows, and perform your vows.’
verses.26: “Therefore hear Yahweh’s word, all Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: ‘Behold, I have sworn by my great name,’ says Yahweh, ‘that my name will no more be named in the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, “As the Lord Yahweh lives.”
verses.27: Behold, I watch over them for evil, and not for good; and all the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt will be consumed by the sword and by the famine, until they are all gone.
verses.28: Those who escape the sword will return out of the land of Egypt into the land of Judah few in number. All the remnant of Judah, who have gone into the land of Egypt to live there, will know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.
verses.29: “‘This will be the sign to you,’ says Yahweh, ‘that I will punish you in this place, that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for evil.’
verses.30: Yahweh says, ‘Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, and into the hand of those who seek his life; as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy, and sought his life.’”

cites.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them.

Yahweh, the God of their fathers, sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place; but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until Yahweh’s wrath arose against his people, until there was no remedy.

4.why: servants the prophets sent daily, rising up early, mocked until there was no remedy

cites.text: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets, and stones those who are sent to her! How often I would have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!

When it was time, he sent a servant to the farmer to get from the farmer his share of the fruit of the vineyard. They took him, beat him, and sent him away empty. Again, he sent another servant to them; and they threw stones at him, wounded him in the head, and sent him away shamefully treated. Again he sent another; and they killed him; and many others, beating some, and killing some. Therefore still having one, his beloved son, he sent him last to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’

4.why: how often would I have gathered you, and a landowner still sending servants

cites.text: Do they provoke me to anger?” says Yahweh. “Don’t they provoke themselves, to the confusion of their own faces?”
But he who sins against me wrongs his own soul. All those who hate me love death.”

7.why: do they provoke me, or themselves to their own confusion - all who hate me love death

cites.text: Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin.
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

7.why: everyone who sins is a bondservant of sin, and the wages of sin is death

cites.text: For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness.
Isaiah cries concerning Israel, “If the number of the children of Israel are as the sand of the sea, it is the remnant who will be saved;

14.why: though the number be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return

cites.text: Yahweh says, “Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, ‘Where is the good way?’ and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls. But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’ I set watchmen over you, saying, ‘Listen to the sound of the trumpet!’ But they said, ‘We will not listen!’
For it is a rebellious people, lying children, children who will not hear Yahweh’s law;

16.why: we will not walk in it, we will not listen - rebellious children unwilling to hear the law

cites.text: The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough, to make cakes to the queen of the sky, and to pour out drink offerings to other gods, that they may provoke me to anger.

He got rid of the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah, and in the places around Jerusalem; those also who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets, and to all the army of the sky.

17.why: the whole household baking cakes for the queen of the sky, and the priests Josiah removed

cites.text: For their mother has played the prostitute. She who conceived them has done shamefully; for she said, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.’ Therefore behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns, and I will build a wall against her, that she can’t find her way. She will follow after her lovers, but she won’t overtake them; and she will seek them, but won’t find them. Then she will say, ‘I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now.’ For she did not know that I gave her the grain, the new wine, and the oil, and multiplied to her silver and gold, which they used for Baal.

and lest you say in your heart, “My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth.” But you shall remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth; that he may establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers, as it is today.

18.why: crediting the lovers for the grain and oil that Yahweh Himself had given

cites.text: When a man vows a vow to Yahweh, or swears an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.
When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow. It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay.

25.why: a vow binds the soul, and better not to vow than to vow and not pay

cites.text: But my people didn’t listen to my voice. Israel desired none of me. So I let them go after the stubbornness of their hearts, that they might walk in their own counsels.

Therefore God also gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to uncleanness, that their bodies should be dishonored among themselves; who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

25.why: so I gave them up to their own hearts' lust - judgment that consists of being permitted

cites.text: There is salvation in none other, for neither is there any other name under heaven, that is given among men, by which we must be saved!”

Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name; that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

26.why: a name withdrawn from one mouth, and the name given above every name

cites.text: Then Yahweh said to me, “You have seen well; for I watch over my word to perform it.”
It will happen that, like as I have watched over them to pluck up and to break down and to overthrow and to destroy and to afflict, so will I watch over them to build and to plant,” says Yahweh.

27.why: the watching branch - I watch over my word to perform it, to break down and to build

cites.text: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

For, “All flesh is like grass, and all of man’s glory like the flower in the grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the Lord’s word endures forever.” This is the word of Good News which was preached to you.

28.why: heaven and earth pass away, but His words do not - the word of the Lord endures forever

cites.text: Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Behold, I will punish Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with her gods, and her kings; even Pharaoh, and those who trust in him. I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants. Afterwards it will be inhabited, as in the days of old,” says Yahweh.

“Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and prophesy against him and against all Egypt. Speak and say, ‘Thus says the Lord Yahweh: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great monster that lies in the middle of his rivers, that has said, ‘My river is my own, and I have made it for myself.’

30.why: Pharaoh and those who trust in him handed over, and the great monster of the Nile

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 45 - A Word for Baruch
chapters.title: A Word for Baruch
keyNotes: The oracle is dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim - about 605 BC, some twenty years before the events of chapters 43 and 44 (Jeremiah 45:1).
Its placement here is deliberate. It closes the scroll the way a scribe signs his own work at the end of the manuscript (Jeremiah 45:1).
That fourth year is the year of chapter 36 - the scroll Baruch wrote, read aloud in the temple, and watched the king cut up and burn (Jeremiah 45:1).
Baruch is a man of standing. His brother Seraiah was Zedekiah's quartermaster, and a clay seal bearing his own name has been recovered - he had a career to lose (Jeremiah 45:2).
Verse 3 preserves the only words of Baruch recorded in Scripture, and they are a complaint: "Woe is me now!" (Jeremiah 45:3).
God quotes the complaint back to him verbatim before answering it. He had heard it exactly as it was said (Jeremiah 45:3).
"Yahweh has added sorrow to my pain" - Baruch does not blame circumstances or enemies. He says the grief came from God, and God does not correct him (Jeremiah 45:3).
The answer begins not with Baruch's trouble but with God's: what I built I am breaking down, what I planted I am plucking up (Jeremiah 45:4).
Those are the verbs of Jeremiah 1:10, and the demolition costs the Builder something. Baruch is being told his sorrow is a share in a larger one (Jeremiah 45:4).
"Do you seek great things for yourself? Don't seek them" is the only rebuke in the oracle, and it is a question rather than a verdict (Jeremiah 45:5).
The timing matters: greatness is not being called sinful, it is being called unavailable. This is not the era for it (Jeremiah 45:5).
The promise given is deliberately small and completely sufficient - "I will let you escape with your life wherever you go" (Jeremiah 45:5).
Life as spoil is this book's particular mercy, given to Ebed-Melech and to those who surrendered, and now to a scribe (Jeremiah 45:5).
"Wherever you go" is quietly generous, and it holds even in Egypt - which is where he ends up, carried off in chapter 43 (Jeremiah 45:5).

intro: Five verses, and they are for one man.

Baruch has been in this book since chapter 32, and he is almost always described by his function: the son of Neriah, who wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah. He buys the field deed and seals it. He takes dictation. He reads the scroll aloud in the temple when Jeremiah cannot go himself, and then hides while Jehoiakim slices it column by column into the brazier. In chapter 43 he is accused of running the prophet, and in the same chapter he is carried into Egypt with him. He is the person in the room whose name is on nothing.

He is a man with prospects, too. His brother Seraiah served as quartermaster in Zedekiah's court, and archaeologists have recovered a clay bulla stamped "belonging to Berechiah son of Neriah the scribe" - though its authenticity is disputed, since it came through the antiquities market rather than an excavation. He came from the class that produced officials. He spent his working life taking down the words of the most hated man in Jerusalem instead.

So in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, with his scroll in ashes and a warrant out for both of them, he says the one thing scripture preserves from his mouth: woe is me now, for Yahweh has added sorrow to my pain; I am weary with my groaning and I find no rest.

Notice three things about the answer he gets. First, God repeats the complaint back to him word for word before responding to it. Baruch had probably said it to himself, or to Jeremiah, on a bad night. It had been heard precisely, and it is quoted with no mockery in it.

Second, the answer does not begin with Baruch. It begins with God: that which I have built I will break down, and that which I have planted I will pluck up. Those are the verbs from Jeremiah's commission, turned here on the Builder's own work. Before God says anything about Baruch's grief, He says that this is costing Him too. The sorrow is not being dismissed. It is being placed inside a larger one.

Third, the correction is a question rather than a sentence. Do you seek great things for yourself? Don't seek them. It is not that ambition is wicked. It is that this is not the season for it, and a man who keeps reaching for a career in a generation like this one will break his hands on it. The word for what he is offered instead is spoil - plunder, what a soldier walks off the field carrying. In a year when everything is being taken, your life will be the thing you get to keep.

It is a small promise. Read in a comfortable century it can sound like a consolation prize. Read standing over the ruins with the temple still smoking, it is enormous. And it comes with the phrase that must have mattered most twenty years later, when he was dragged across the Egyptian border by men who blamed him for the whole thing: wherever you go.

The God who was in the middle of dismantling a nation stopped, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, to answer one exhausted man who had not asked for anything except to be allowed to feel it. He never told him the pain was unwarranted. He told him it was shared, and that he would come out of it alive.

verses.1: The message that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the mouth of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, saying,
verses.2: “Yahweh, the God of Israel, says to you, Baruch:
verses.3: ‘You said, “Woe is me now! For Yahweh has added sorrow to my pain! I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.”’
verses.4: “You shall tell him, Yahweh says: ‘Behold, that which I have built, I will break down, and that which I have planted I will pluck up; and this in the whole land.
verses.5: Do you seek great things for yourself? Don’t seek them; for, behold, I will bring evil on all flesh,’ says Yahweh; ‘but I will let you escape with your life wherever you go.’”

cites.text: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying, “Take a scroll of a book, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah, even to this day. It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I intend to do to them; that they may each return from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.” Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah; and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all Yahweh’s words, which he had spoken to him, on a scroll of a book.
The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (the same was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon),

1.why: the fourth year of Jehoiakim - the year of the scroll, and of Nebuchadnezzar's first year

cites.text: I, Tertius, who write the letter, greet you in the Lord.
For God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work and the labor of love which you showed toward his name, in that you served the saints, and still do serve them.

1.why: Tertius who wrote the epistle, and a God not unrighteous to forget your work

cites.text: Woe is me, my mother, that you have borne me, a man of strife, and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have not lent, neither have men lent to me; yet every one of them curses me.
I am weary with my groaning. Every night I flood my bed. I drench my couch with my tears.

3.why: woe is me, my mother, that you bore me - and a bed soaked with weeping

cites.text: Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.
For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.

3.why: your Father knows what you need before you ask, and a High Priest who feels our weakness

cites.text: Behold, I have today set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”
It will happen that, like as I have watched over them to pluck up and to break down and to overthrow and to destroy and to afflict, so will I watch over them to build and to plant,” says Yahweh.

4.why: to pluck up and to break down, to build and to plant - the commission verbs, reversed

cites.text: For he does not afflict willingly, nor grieve the children of men.
When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it,

4.why: He does not afflict willingly, and He wept over the city as He said what must come

cites.text: Yahweh, my heart isn’t haughty, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.

chapters.title: Carchemish, and the River That Called Itself a Flood
keyNotes: Chapters 46 through 51 form a distinct block - "concerning the nations" - in which the God of a defeated little kingdom claims jurisdiction over the whole map (Jeremiah 46:1).
The first oracle is dated to Carchemish in 605 BC, the battle that ended Assyria and Egypt as world powers and installed Babylon in their place (Jeremiah 46:2).
That is the same fourth year of Jehoiakim as the burned scroll of chapter 36 and the word to Baruch in chapter 45 - a very loud year (Jeremiah 46:2).
The opening is a mustering order shouted at an army that is already lost: harness, polish, put on the mail. The arming is the joke (Jeremiah 46:3-4).
Verse 5 breaks the rhythm with a stunned question - "Why have I seen it?" - as though the prophet is watching the rout in real time (Jeremiah 46:5).
"Terror is on every side" is Jeremiah's own signature phrase, the words that were used to taunt him in chapter 20, now pointed outward at Egypt (Jeremiah 46:5).
Egypt is drawn as the Nile in flood, rising to cover the earth - imperial ambition described in the language of the river Egypt worshipped (Jeremiah 46:7-8).
The mercenary roll call of Cush, Put, and the Ludim is an army money can buy, and money does not make men stand (Jeremiah 46:9).
The battle is called a sacrifice, and the one it is offered to is Yahweh of Armies. The day of vengeance is His, not Nebuchadnezzar's (Jeremiah 46:10).
"Go up into Gilead, and take balm, virgin daughter of Egypt" turns Jeremiah's own famous question about Judah around and asks it of Egypt: there is no healing (Jeremiah 46:11).
The second oracle jumps forward decades to Babylon's invasion of Egypt itself, naming Migdol, Memphis, and Tahpanhes - the very towns the refugees of chapter 44 settled in (Jeremiah 46:13-14).
"Why are your strong ones swept away?" carries a probable pun on Apis, the bull-god of Memphis: the divine bull knocked flat because Yahweh pushed him (Jeremiah 46:15).
The hired troops decide to go home mid-campaign. Foreign soldiers will not die for someone else's empire (Jeremiah 46:16).
Their verdict on Pharaoh is devastating and comes from his own payroll: "but a noise; he has let the appointed time pass by" (Jeremiah 46:17).
Egypt is a very beautiful heifer, sleek and well fed, stung into panic by something out of the north; her mercenaries are calves of the stall, fattened and useless (Jeremiah 46:20-21).
Egypt's collapse sounds like a snake slipping away through the undergrowth while the woodcutters come in with axes (Jeremiah 46:22-23).
Then the tone breaks: "Afterwards it will be inhabited, as in the days of old." Even Egypt gets a restoration clause (Jeremiah 46:26).
Verses 27 and 28 turn from Egypt to Jacob, repeating almost word for word the comfort of chapter 30 in the middle of a foreign-nation oracle (Jeremiah 46:27).
The distinction the whole block rests on is stated plainly: a full end of the nations, no full end of you - correction in measure (Jeremiah 46:28).

intro: Something changes here, and it is worth naming before reading a word of it.

For forty-five chapters this book has been an argument inside one family. Judah, Jerusalem, the temple, the kings, the priests, the false prophets. Now the camera pulls back, and the God who has been pleading with a small hill kingdom starts naming the cities of Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam and Babylon. Judah has just been reduced to rubble by an empire. And from inside that rubble, her prophet announces the fate of empires.

That is either delusional or it is the most important claim in the book. Jeremiah has been saying all along that Nebuchadnezzar is a servant and not a sovereign. Chapters 46 through 51 are where the claim is cashed out across the whole map.

The first oracle is Carchemish, 605 BC - a battle most people have never heard of that rearranged the ancient world. Pharaoh Necoh marched north to prop up the last of Assyria; Nebuchadnezzar met him at the Euphrates and destroyed him. Assyria ended. Egypt withdrew behind its border and stayed there. Babylon inherited everything. It happened in the fourth year of Jehoiakim - the same year Baruch wrote the scroll, the same year the king cut it into the fire, the same year God told one tired scribe not to seek great things for himself.

Watch how the poem is built. It opens as a parade-ground order: harness the horses, polish the spears, put on the coats of mail. Then verse 5 stops mid-stride - why have I seen it? - and the whole armament collapses into men fleeing without looking back. The phrase used for their panic is magor missabib, terror on every side, which is Jeremiah's own phrase. It is what Pashhur was renamed in chapter 20 and what the mob shouted at Jeremiah to mock him. Here it lands on Egypt.

Then notice the image in verses 7 and 8. Egypt rises like the Nile. That is not a random metaphor - the Nile was a god, and the annual flood was the source of everything Egypt had. The empire is described in the exact terms of the thing it worshipped: I will rise up, I will cover the earth. And the river runs out of its bank.

But the chapter does not end where a judgement oracle should end. Verse 26 says Egypt will be inhabited again, as in the days of old. And then verses 27 and 28 turn away from Egypt entirely and speak to Jacob, in words lifted almost intact out of chapter 30: don't be afraid, I am with you, I will make a full end of the nations but not of you.

That last distinction is the hinge of the whole section, and it is easy to get wrong. It is not that Judah is spared what the nations get. Judah got it first and got it worst. The difference is the word measure. The nations are ended. Judah is corrected. Being loved by God is not the absence of discipline; it is the presence of a limit on it.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 47 - The Sword of Yahweh, and the Question It Will Not Answer
chapters.title: The Sword of Yahweh, and the Question It Will Not Answer
keyNotes: Seven verses for Philistia - the oldest enemy on Israel's list, fought since the days of the judges and now dispatched in a single short poem (Jeremiah 47:1).
The dating is a raid recorded nowhere else in Scripture: "before Pharaoh struck Gaza" (Jeremiah 47:1).
The invader is not described as an army but as water - a flood rising out of the north, impersonal, and impossible to fight (Jeremiah 47:2).
"Waters out of the north" is the same direction as the boiling pot of chapter 1 and the same threat, now running along the coast instead of into the hills (Jeremiah 47:2).
Verse 3 is among the most terrible images in the book: fathers do not turn back for their own children, because their hands have gone slack with fear (Jeremiah 47:3).
Tyre and Sidon lose their last help. The Philistine ports were the coastal alliance's remaining support, and the whole seaboard goes together (Jeremiah 47:4).
Caphtor is Crete. Scripture remembers that the Philistines were immigrants and names their homeland even while announcing their end (Jeremiah 47:4).
Shaved heads and cut flesh are the mourning rites of the coast - the same forbidden practices worn by the pilgrims murdered at Mizpah (Jeremiah 47:5).
Verse 6 gives someone a voice - prophet, or victim, or the land itself - pleading directly with the weapon: how long? Go back in your scabbard, rest, be still (Jeremiah 47:6).
The plea is one of the most human sentences in the prophets, and it is refused (Jeremiah 47:6).
The refusal is not cruelty but obedience: the sword has been given a command and an appointment, and it cannot be quiet until the work is done (Jeremiah 47:7).
Philistia gets no restoration clause. Egypt is promised an afterwards and Moab a latter day; this chapter simply ends (Jeremiah 47:7).

intro: Seven verses, and one of them will not leave a reader alone.

Philistia is the oldest name on Israel's enemies list. Samson, the ark at Ashdod, Goliath in the valley of Elah, David hiding at Gath - centuries of it. Here the whole story is closed out in a single short poem, which says something about how history looks from where Jeremiah is standing.

The invader is not drawn as an army. It is water. Waters rise up out of the north and become an overflowing stream, and cover the land and the city and everyone in it. An army can be fought. A flood cannot; a person is either in its way or not. And north is the direction the boiling pot was tipped from back in chapter 1 - the same threat, now running down the coastal plain instead of up into the hills.

Then verse 3, which is the verse that stays. The noise of the hooves and the chariots and the rumbling wheels comes on, and the fathers do not look back to their children for feebleness of hands. Fathers running, and not turning around for their own children - not because they do not love them, but because terror has emptied their arms. Jeremiah does not comment on it. He puts it down and moves on, and the restraint is what makes it unbearable.

And then verse 6, where somebody finally speaks. The text does not say who. It could be the prophet; it could be a Philistine; it could be the land itself. Whoever it is turns and addresses the weapon directly: you sword of Yahweh, how long will it be before you are quiet? Put yourself back into your scabbard; rest, and be still.
That is the prayer every honest person has prayed while watching a catastrophe. Enough. Stop now. Go back in the sheath.

And it is refused. How can you be quiet, since Yahweh has given you a command? Against Ashkelon, and against the seashore, there has he appointed it. The sword is not being cruel. It is being obedient. It has an assignment and a location, and it cannot rest in the middle of them.

The discomfort of that is better sat with than resolved quickly. This chapter offers no restoration clause - Egypt gets an afterwards, Moab gets a latter day, Philistia gets nothing written down. And the question "how long" is not answered here. It is answered elsewhere and much later, by another voice on a hill saying it is finished - but Jeremiah is not given that yet, and neither are the people in this poem.

What is worth noticing is that the question was allowed to be asked. Nobody rebukes the one who pleads with the sword. Scripture keeps the plea in the text, unanswered, sitting right next to the judgement. There is room in this book for asking God to stop.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 48 - Moab Settled on His Lees
chapters.title: Moab Settled on His Lees
keyNotes: Forty-seven verses - the longest oracle against any single nation in Jeremiah, spent on a small kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea (Jeremiah 48:1).
Moab descends from Lot, Abraham's nephew. This is a quarrel between relatives, which is part of why it runs so long (Jeremiah 48:1).
The place names are real towns with real streets - Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Dibon, Aroer, Kerioth, Kir Heres. This is judgment with addresses (Jeremiah 48:21-24).
"You also, Madmen, will be brought to silence" is a pun: the town Madmen and the Hebrew damam, to be struck dumb (Jeremiah 48:2).
Moab trusted "in your works and in your treasures," and the confidence is the first thing confiscated (Jeremiah 48:7).
Chemosh goes into exile with his priests and princes - a national god loaded onto a cart and carried away by somebody else's soldiers (Jeremiah 48:7).
Verse 10 is the hardest sentence in the chapter, a curse on doing Yahweh's work negligently, spoken over the invaders about the thoroughness of their assignment (Jeremiah 48:10).
The wine image at verse 11 is the heart of the whole oracle: Moab has settled on his lees and has never been emptied from vessel to vessel (Jeremiah 48:11).
Wine left standing on its sediment keeps its taste but never clarifies. Undisturbed comfort is being named as the disease, not the reward (Jeremiah 48:11).
Moab had never been deported. Three hundred years of not being moved produced a nation whose scent had never had to change (Jeremiah 48:11).
"Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel" - a comparison with a barb in it, since Israel's own shrine failed exactly the same way (Jeremiah 48:13).
Moab's particular offense against Israel was mockery at her fall: "as often as you speak of him, you shake your head" (Jeremiah 48:27).
Pride is named four times in a single verse - loftiness, pride, arrogance, and haughtiness of heart - as though one word could not carry it (Jeremiah 48:29).
"I know his wrath, that it is nothing; his boastings have done nothing." The deflation is almost tender (Jeremiah 48:30).
And then the turn that no one expects in a judgment speech: "Therefore I will wail for Moab. Yes, I will cry out for all Moab" (Jeremiah 48:31).
"My heart sounds for Moab like pipes" - the reed flute of a funeral procession, playing inside the heart of the God who is bringing the funeral (Jeremiah 48:36).
Verses 29 through 38 track Isaiah 15 and 16 closely. Jeremiah picks up an older lament for Moab and finishes it (Jeremiah 48:29-38).
Terror, the pit, and the snare are three escapes that each empty into the next trap (Jeremiah 48:43-44).
The judgment closes with mercy anyway: "Yet I will reverse the captivity of Moab in the latter days" (Jeremiah 48:47).
That clause is worth remembering alongside Ruth, a Moabite woman who became the great-grandmother of David (Jeremiah 48:47).

intro: Forty-seven verses for Moab. That is longer than the first movement of the oracle against Babylon, longer than anything said here about Egypt, and vastly longer than the seven verses Philistia was given. A small plateau kingdom east of the Dead Sea, and God will not stop talking about it.

Part of the reason is family. Moab is Lot's son - the child of Abraham's nephew. Israel and Moab are cousins, and the history between them is long and bad: Balak hiring Balaam to curse Israel, the women of Moab at Baal Peor, centuries of border war. And running the other way, quietly, a Moabite widow named Ruth who said your people will be my people, and became the great- grandmother of David. Both of those are true about Moab at once.

The verse everything turns on is verse 11, and it is a winemaker's line. Moab has been at ease from his youth, and he has settled on his lees, and has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither has he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed.

Here is what that means in a cellar. New wine is left on its lees - the sediment - for a while, because the contact adds body. But it cannot stay there. It has to be racked: poured carefully off into a fresh vessel, leaving the sediment behind, and then again, and again. Wine that is never racked keeps its strength and never becomes clear. It stays thick and cloudy, and eventually the very sediment that gave it character begins to spoil it.

Moab had never been racked. Every other nation in the region had been overrun, deported, resettled and humiliated. Moab sat on its plateau for three hundred years, prosperous, undisturbed and unchanged. And God names that undisturbedness not as a blessing but as the reason judgement is required.

That should land somewhere uncomfortable. A long stretch of ease is usually read as evidence of favour. This chapter reads it as a warning. "His taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed" sounds like a compliment and is not one. Nothing had ever happened to Moab that required Moab to become anything different.

Out of that comfort came pride, and verse 29 stacks the words up because one will not hold it: loftiness, pride, arrogance, haughtiness of heart. And the specific form it took was mockery. Verse 27: wasn't Israel a derision to you? As often as you speak of him, you shake your head. When Jerusalem fell, Moab enjoyed it. That is the sin that gets named.

And then verse 31 arrives and does something a judgement oracle is not supposed to do. Therefore I will wail for Moab. Yes, I will cry out for all Moab. Not Jeremiah - Yahweh. Verse 36: my heart sounds for Moab like pipes. The pipe is the reed flute of a funeral procession, the instrument hired mourners played behind a coffin. God says that sound is going on inside Him. For Moab. For a pagan nation that worshipped Chemosh and laughed at Jerusalem, and that He Himself is in the act of breaking.

Let that reorder what judgement is taken to mean. This is not a God who enjoys any of it. He grieved over Judah in chapter 42; He weeps over Moab here; He will weep over Jerusalem again from a donkey six centuries later. And He ends even this chapter with a door left open: yet I will reverse the captivity of Moab in the latter days.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 49 - Five Nations, and the Doors Left Open
chapters.title: Five Nations, and the Doors Left Open
keyNotes: Five oracles in one chapter - Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, and Elam - moving outward from the neighbours next door to the edge of the known world (Jeremiah 49:1-39).
Ammon's offense is annexation. When Assyria deported the tribes east of the Jordan, Ammon moved into Gad and stayed (Jeremiah 49:1).
"Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir?" is estate language - the question you ask when someone occupies a house while the family is away (Jeremiah 49:1).
Malcam is Milcom, Ammon's god, and he goes into captivity with his priests and princes exactly as Chemosh did in the previous chapter (Jeremiah 49:3).
Ammon's confidence was geography and money - a well-watered valley, full treasuries, and the question "Who will come to me?" (Jeremiah 49:4).
And then verse 6 leaves the door open anyway: afterward I will reverse the captivity of the children of Ammon (Jeremiah 49:6).
Edom's boast was wisdom. Teman was proverbial for it, and Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite (Jeremiah 49:7).
The judgment on Edom is deliberately more thorough than either harvest or robbery: gleaners leave grapes and thieves stop when satisfied, but Esau is stripped bare (Jeremiah 49:9-10).
Verse 11 is astonishing where it sits: "Leave your fatherless children. I will preserve them alive. Let your widows trust in me" - said to Edom (Jeremiah 49:11).
The cup argument is a fortiori: if those who did not deserve it had to drink, on what grounds would you be excused? (Jeremiah 49:12).
Edom lived in the clefts of the rock - the red sandstone country around Petra - and the text names exactly what that altitude did to them (Jeremiah 49:16).
Damascus is the oldest continuously inhabited city on earth, and God calls it "the city of praise, the city of my joy" while announcing its fall (Jeremiah 49:25).
Kedar and Hazor are not a city-state but tent-dwelling Arab clans - "a nation that is at ease, that dwells without care, that has neither gates nor bars" (Jeremiah 49:31).
Their very defenselessness is what makes them a target. Nebuchadnezzar takes counsel against people with nothing to besiege (Jeremiah 49:30-31).
Elam lies east of Babylon, at the outer edge of the map, and its oracle is dated to the beginning of Zedekiah's reign (Jeremiah 49:34).
"I will set my throne in Elam" is the boldest sentence in the chapter - Yahweh planting His seat in the homeland of a people Judah had never met (Jeremiah 49:38).
Three of these oracles end with a reversal - Ammon, Elam, and Moab just before them. Edom and Damascus are given none (Jeremiah 49:6, 49:39).

intro: Five nations, and the chapter works outward like a stone dropped in water. Ammon is next door. Edom is the cousin south of the Dead Sea. Damascus is up the trade road. Kedar and Hazor are tent camps out in the Arabian desert. And Elam is past Babylon entirely, at the edge of anything a man in Jerusalem would have heard of.

Ammon is charged with taking what was not theirs. When Assyria deported the tribes east of the Jordan, Gad's territory sat empty, and Ammon moved in and never left. The opening question is legal and it is bitter: has Israel no sons, has he no heir? You occupied a house because you assumed the family was not coming back.

Then Edom, and this is where the chapter does something worth slowing down for. Edom is Esau - Jacob's twin, the brother who was cheated and who never forgot it. The judgement is severe and total: grape gatherers leave gleanings and thieves stop when they have enough, but Esau is stripped bare, his hiding places uncovered, his offspring gone.
And then, dropped into the middle of that, verse 11. Leave your fatherless children. I will preserve them alive. Let your widows trust in me.

Read that again and notice who is speaking to whom. This is Yahweh, in the middle of dismantling Edom, telling Edomite men that He will look after their orphans and inviting Edomite widows to trust Him. There is no condition attached to it. It is the same God who is called elsewhere a father of the fatherless, and here He extends the title across a border, into a nation He is judging, to the children of men who hated His people.

Kedar is worth a moment as well. Nebuchadnezzar takes his army out into the desert to attack people who live in tents - a nation that is at ease, that dwells without care, that has neither gates nor bars. There is nothing to besiege. No walls, no treasury, no throne. Camels and curtains and flocks. Empires do that. When there is nothing left worth taking they will still go and take what there is.

And it is worth counting the doors. Moab was given one at the end of the previous chapter. Ammon gets one in verse 6, Elam in verse 39. Egypt was given one in chapter 46. Not everyone here receives a latter-day clause - Edom does not, Damascus does not - and scripture offers no explanation for the difference. But the pattern is unmistakable and it runs in one direction: outward, toward people who were never in the covenant at all.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 50 - The Hammer of the Whole Earth
chapters.title: The Hammer of the Whole Earth
keyNotes: Chapters 50 and 51 are the longest sustained oracle in the book - over a hundred verses aimed at Babylon (Jeremiah 50:1).
The paradox is the whole point. Jeremiah spent forty years telling Judah to submit to Babylon, and here he spends a hundred verses saying Babylon is finished (Jeremiah 50:1).
Bel and Merodach are named - Marduk, the city god whose statue was paraded through the streets at the New Year festival (Jeremiah 50:2).
The destroyer comes "out of the north," which is the exact phrase used for Babylon coming at Judah. The terror is handed back to its author (Jeremiah 50:3).
Verses 4 and 5 turn immediately homeward: Israel and Judah together, going and weeping, asking the road to Zion (Jeremiah 50:4).
"Come, and join yourselves to Yahweh in an everlasting covenant that will not be forgotten" - the new covenant of chapter 31, now in the exiles' own mouths (Jeremiah 50:5).
"My people have been lost sheep... They have forgotten their resting place." The shepherds are blamed and the sheep are still lost (Jeremiah 50:6).
Babylon's legal defense is quoted and rejected: we are not guilty, because they had sinned against Yahweh. Being the instrument is not the same as being innocent (Jeremiah 50:7).
Verse 11 names the actual charge, and it is not the conquest. It is the enjoyment of it - glad, rejoicing, wanton as a heifer, neighing like stallions (Jeremiah 50:11).
Verse 20 is one of the great verses of the book: the iniquity of Israel will be sought for, and there will be none (Jeremiah 50:20).
The searching is deliberate. Someone goes looking for the sin, and the sin is not there - not overlooked, not excused, not found (Jeremiah 50:20).
"I will pardon them whom I leave as a remnant" ties the whole book's remnant thread to forgiveness rather than survival (Jeremiah 50:20).
Merathaim and Pekod are real districts of southern Babylonia whose names double as puns - "double rebellion" and "punishment" (Jeremiah 50:21).
"How the hammer of the whole earth is cut apart and broken!" - the tool gets broken after the work is done (Jeremiah 50:23).
"I have laid a snare for you, and you are also taken, Babylon, and you weren't aware." The empire is caught by something it never saw coming (Jeremiah 50:24).
"Their Redeemer is strong: Yahweh of Armies is his name. He will thoroughly plead their cause." The word is go'el - the kinsman who buys his relative back (Jeremiah 50:34).
Verses 35 to 38 hammer "a sword is on" five times and then end with "a drought is on her waters" - a city built on canals, dried out (Jeremiah 50:35-38).
Verses 44 to 46 repeat the Edom oracle of chapter 49 almost word for word. The same sentence fits any empire you care to name (Jeremiah 50:44-46).

intro: Hold the two halves of Jeremiah's message together, because this chapter is where they finally meet.

For forty years he told Judah to submit to Babylon. Put your neck under the yoke. Serve the king of Babylon and live. Build houses in exile, plant gardens, seek the peace of the city. He was called a traitor for it, thrown in a cistern for it, and nearly executed for it.
And here are a hundred verses saying Babylon is finished.

Both were always true, and the tension between them is the discipline of this whole book. Submit to what God has permitted; do not mistake it for what God approves. Babylon was the rod in His hand, and the rod gets broken too.

Look at what Babylon is actually charged with, because it is not the conquest. Verse 11: because you are glad, because you rejoice, you who plunder my heritage, because you are wanton as a heifer that treads out the grain. The crime is the enjoyment. They were sent, and they had a good time doing it. Verse 7 records their defence in their own words - we are not guilty, because they have sinned against Yahweh - and God does not accept it. Being an instrument does not make anyone innocent of how they handled the job.

Then verse 20, which should be read slowly. In those days and in that time, the iniquity of Israel will be sought for, and there will be none; also the sins of Judah, and they won't be found; for I will pardon them whom I leave as a remnant.

Notice the mechanism. Someone goes looking. There is a search, deliberate and thorough, for the sin of the people whose sin has occupied forty-nine chapters of this book - the idolatry, the children burned in Hinnom, the broken covenant, the murdered prophets, the burned scroll, the queen of the sky in the kitchens of Egypt. All of it. And the search comes back empty. Not excused, not minimised, not lost in the paperwork. Not there.

The other word worth sitting with is in verse 34: Redeemer. Go'el. It is a family term rather than a legal one. The go'el is the relative obliged to buy you back when you have sold yourself into slavery, to redeem the land you had to sell, to stand up in court on your behalf when you cannot. Their Redeemer is strong. The strength matters, because the people being redeemed have none.

Put verse 6 and verse 19 side by side. My people have been lost sheep; their shepherds have caused them to go astray; they have forgotten their resting place. And then: I will bring Israel again to his pasture, and his soul will be satisfied. The shepherds failed. The sheep are still His.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 51 - A Stone Tied to a Scroll
chapters.title: A Stone Tied to a Scroll
keyNotes: "Babylon has been a golden cup in Yahweh's hand" - beautiful, valuable, held by God, and full of something that drove the nations mad (Jeremiah 51:7).
Verse 9 contains a line nobody expects in an oracle of doom: "We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed" (Jeremiah 51:9).
The Medes are named as the agent decades before Cyrus, and named again in verse 28 with their governors and deputies (Jeremiah 51:11, 51:28).
The vengeance is specifically "the vengeance of his temple" - the burned house is being answered for by name (Jeremiah 51:11).
Verses 15 through 19 lift the creation hymn of chapter 10 word for word and set it against the idols of Babylon (Jeremiah 51:15-19).
The contrast is the whole theology of the book in two sentences: goldsmiths disappointed by their images, and "the portion of Jacob is not like these" (Jeremiah 51:17-19).
"You are my battle ax and weapons of war" - Babylon addressed as God's tool inside the very chapter that breaks the tool (Jeremiah 51:20).

The breaking list is relentless and deliberately indiscriminate, down to the young man and the virgin, the shepherd and his flock. War does not sort people, and the poem will not pretend otherwise (Jeremiah 51:21-23).
Babylon is called a "destroying mountain" that will be rolled down and burned, and from whose rubble no one will ever take a cornerstone (Jeremiah 51:25-26).
Verse 34 hands the microphone to Zion: Nebuchadnezzar "has made me an empty vessel... has swallowed me up" (Jeremiah 51:34).
Verse 44 answers her directly - "I will bring out of his mouth that which he has swallowed up" (Jeremiah 51:44).
Babylon falls at a feast, drunk, sleeping a sleep it does not wake from - which is remarkably close to the night Daniel records (Jeremiah 51:39, 51:57).
"Sheshach" in verse 41 is an athbash cipher for Babel: the name written backwards through the alphabet, a scribe's code (Jeremiah 51:41).
"My people, go away from the middle of her" is quoted almost exactly in Revelation 18 (Jeremiah 51:45).

The closing act is a piece of theatre performed a thousand miles away: Seraiah - Baruch's brother - carries the scroll to Babylon, reads it out, ties a stone to it, and throws it into the Euphrates (Jeremiah 51:59-63).
Nobody would have been listening. The point was not the audience; it was that the word was delivered to the address it was written to (Jeremiah 51:61-62).
"Thus far are the words of Jeremiah" - the book signs itself off, and everything after this is appendix (Jeremiah 51:64).

intro: The image in verse 7 deserves a minute of its own. Babylon has been a golden cup in Yahweh's hand, who made all the earth drunk.

Everything is in that sentence. The cup is gold - genuinely magnificent, the greatest city in the world, with processional ways and hanging gardens and a library of astronomy. It is in Yahweh's hand; He is the one holding it and He is the one pouring. And what comes out of it makes the nations mad. Beauty, usefulness, divine appointment and lunacy, all in one object.

Then verse 9, which is the strangest line in the chapter: we would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed. Forsake her, and let us each go into his own country. Somebody tried. The verse does not say who - the exiles who lived there, perhaps, or the nations, or the prophets generally. But healing was attempted, and it failed, and only then is she left. That is not how a triumphal poem about an enemy's destruction is supposed to go.

Watch what verses 15 through 19 do. They are word for word out of chapter 10 - He made the earth by His power, established the world by His wisdom, stretched out the heavens; every goldsmith is put to shame by his image, for his molten image is falsehood and there is no breath in them. In chapter 10 Jeremiah preached that to Judah, warning them not to be impressed by Babylonian religion. Here he preaches the identical sermon at Babylon itself. He did not need a new argument. The idols were always empty; it simply took an empire falling for anyone to see it.
And then the ending, which is one of the most quietly extraordinary scenes in scripture.

Zedekiah goes to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign, and Seraiah goes with him as chief quartermaster. Seraiah is Baruch's brother - another son of Neriah, another man from the scribal class carrying paper for Jeremiah. And Jeremiah gives him a scroll with all of this written in it and tells him: when you get there, read it out loud. Then tie a stone to it and throw it in the river, and say, thus will Babylon sink.

Think about performing that. You are in the capital of the empire that owns your country. The walls are enormous. Nobody is listening to you. You read out a poem announcing the end of the place, and then you walk down to the Euphrates and drop a rock-weighted scroll into it in front of nobody in particular, and go home.
It was not a demonstration. It was a delivery. The word had an address, and Jeremiah made sure it got there.

And notice the sentence that comes immediately after: thus far are the words of Jeremiah. Forty years of preaching, and it ends with a scroll sinking in a river in a country he never visited. He did not live to see a single line of this fulfilled. Babylon fell in 539, long after he was gone. He delivered it anyway.

chapters.title: The Appendix, and a Table in Babylon
keyNotes: Chapter 52 is an appendix. Verse 64 of the previous chapter already said "thus far are the words of Jeremiah," so someone else added this (Jeremiah 52:1).
It is nearly identical to 2 Kings 24:18 through 25:30, attached here as documentation - the receipts for everything the book has been claiming (Jeremiah 52:1).
Zedekiah's mother is Hamutal "the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah" - a different Jeremiah, one of the quiet coincidences of the chapter (Jeremiah 52:1).
The dates are given to the day: the tenth day of the tenth month, the ninth day of the fourth month, the tenth day of the fifth month. Record-keeping is a form of grief (Jeremiah 52:4, 52:6, 52:12).
Eighteen months of siege end in famine and a breach in the wall at night, with the army running for the Arabah (Jeremiah 52:5-7).
The last thing Zedekiah ever sees is the execution of his sons. Then his eyes are put out (Jeremiah 52:10-11).
Two prophecies that sounded contradictory both come true precisely: he would see the king of Babylon eye to eye, and he would be brought to Babylon without seeing it (Jeremiah 52:11).
The temple, the palace, and every great house are burned, and the walls of Jerusalem pulled down all around (Jeremiah 52:13-14).
Then the inventory - pots, shovels, snuffers, basins, spoons, fire pans, lamp stands - listed one by one, because you count what you have lost (Jeremiah 52:18-19).
The two bronze pillars are measured one final time before they are broken up for scrap metal (Jeremiah 52:21-23).
The ninety-six pomegranates on each capital get their own verse. Somebody remembered them (Jeremiah 52:23).
Seraiah the chief priest - not the Seraiah of chapter 51 - is executed at Riblah with the second priest and the doorkeepers (Jeremiah 52:24-27).
The deportation totals are startlingly small: 3,023 then 832 then 745, "all the people were four thousand six hundred" (Jeremiah 52:28-30).
Whatever those figures counted, a nation has been reduced to a line item in an imperial ledger (Jeremiah 52:30).

And then, with no warning, the last four verses. In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity, Evil-Merodach "lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and released him from prison" (Jeremiah 52:31).
He speaks kindly to him, sets his throne above the other captive kings, and changes his prison clothes (Jeremiah 52:32-33).
"Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life," with a daily allowance until his death (Jeremiah 52:33-34).
The book of Jeremiah ends with a son of David out of prison, in clean clothes, eating at a king's table. Nothing is restored. But the line is not extinguished (Jeremiah 52:34).

intro: This chapter is not Jeremiah's. The last line of the previous chapter said so plainly: thus far are the words of Jeremiah. Someone else - an editor, a later scribe, someone who wanted the file complete - attached a copy of the end of 2 Kings and let the book close on it.

It reads like an official record, and for most of its length that is exactly what it is. Dates to the day. Names of officers. Measurements of pillars. Numbers of deportees. It is the most unemotional chapter in a book that has been weeping for fifty-one chapters, and the flatness is its own kind of grief.

Look at verses 18 and 19 particularly. Pots, shovels, snuffers, basins, spoons, fire pans, lamp stands, bowls. Someone sat down and wrote out the contents of a burned building. And then verse 23: ninety-six pomegranates on the sides, a hundred on the network all around. Somebody counted the decorations on a pillar that no longer existed. That is what people do. When something has been taken, the mind goes back over the inventory.

The numbers in verses 28 to 30 stop a reader as well. Three thousand and twenty-three. Eight hundred and thirty-two. Seven hundred and forty-five. Four thousand six hundred in total. Whatever exactly those figures counted - most likely heads of households rather than every person, since Kings gives much larger totals - the effect is the same. A kingdom with a temple and a throne and four hundred years of history has become a four-digit entry in somebody's ledger.
And then verse 31 arrives and the chapter does something nobody asked it to.

Thirty-seven years into the captivity a new king comes to the throne in Babylon, and for no stated reason he sends for Jehoiachin - the boy king who surrendered at eighteen and had been in prison ever since. Evil-Merodach lifted up the head of Jehoiachin. He speaks kindly to him. He sets his throne above the thrones of the other captive kings. He takes away the prison clothes. And Jehoiachin eats bread before him continually, on a daily allowance, all the days of his life.
That is how the book of Jeremiah ends.

It is not restoration. The temple is still ash, the land is still empty, the man is still in Babylon, and he never goes home. But he is out of the cell, he is fed, he is clothed, and he is a son of David. In chapter 22 God said of this same man that no descendant of his would prosper sitting on David's throne - and here is the line, alive, in the enemy's capital, eating. Both things are true, and Matthew's genealogy runs straight through Jehoiachin.

Hold that ending for what it is. Nothing is fixed. Everything Jeremiah warned about happened, exactly, down to the day. And the final sentence of the whole prophecy is about a man being given bread every day until he died. Not a throne. Not a temple. Bread, daily, for the rest of his life - which is, as it turns out, the thing we were taught to ask for.

verses.1: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign. He reigned eleven years in Jerusalem: and his mother’s name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
verses.2: He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.
verses.3: For through Yahweh’s anger this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out from his presence. Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.
verses.4: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and encamped against it; and they built forts against it round about.
verses.5: So the city was besieged to the eleventh year of king Zedekiah.
verses.6: In the fourth month, in the ninth day of the month, the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land.
verses.7: Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled, and went out of the city by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, which was by the king’s garden. Now the Chaldeans were against the city all around. The men of war went toward the Arabah,
verses.8: but the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.
verses.9: Then they took the king, and carried him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; and he pronounced judgment on him.

verses.27: The king of Babylon struck them, and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried away captive out of his land.
verses.28: This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year, three thousand twenty-three Jews;
verses.29: in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty-two persons;
verses.30: in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred forty-five people: all the people were four thousand six hundred.
verses.31: In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, in the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evilmerodach king of Babylon, in the first year of his reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and released him from prison.
verses.32: He spoke kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babylon,
verses.33: and changed his prison garments. Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life.
verses.34: For his allowance, there was a continual allowance given him by the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.

cites.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, according to all that Jehoiakim had done. For through the anger of Yahweh, this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out from his presence. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem, and besieged it. In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city.

1.why: the same account in Kings, and the fall already narrated in chapter 39

I will also spread my net on him, and he will be taken in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon to the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it, though he will die there.

11.why: he would see the king of Babylon eye to eye, and be brought there without seeing it

cites.text: For he fashioned the two pillars of brass, eighteen cubits high apiece; and a line of twelve cubits encircled either of them. He made two capitals of molten brass, to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits.

For Yahweh of Armies says concerning the pillars, concerning the sea, concerning the bases, and concerning the rest of the vessels that are left in this city, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon didn’t take when he carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, from Jerusalem to Babylon, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem; yes, Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says concerning the vessels that are left in Yahweh’s house, and in the house of the king of Judah, and at Jerusalem: ‘They will be carried to Babylon, and there they will be, until the day that I visit them,’ says Yahweh; ‘then I will bring them up, and restore them to this place.’”

17.why: the pillars Solomon cast, and the promise that the vessels would go and one day return

I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb, are its temple.

19.why: the vessels brought out again by Cyrus, and a city that finally needs no temple

Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life; and for his allowance, there was a continual allowance given him from the king, every day a portion, all the days of his life.

“As I live,” says Yahweh, “though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet on my right hand, yet would I pluck you from there. I would give you into the hand of those who seek your life, and into the hand of them of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of the Chaldeans. I will cast you out with your mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born; and there you will die. But to the land to which their soul longs to return, there they will not return.” Is this man Coniah a despised broken vessel? Is he a vessel in which no one delights? Why are they cast out, he and his offspring, and cast into a land which they don’t know? O earth, earth, earth, hear Yahweh’s word! Yahweh says, “Record this man as childless, a man who will not prosper in his days; for no more will a man of his offspring prosper, sitting on David’s throne, and ruling in Judah.”

31.why: the lifter up of my head, and a lamp kept burning for David in Jerusalem

33.why: a table prepared in the presence of enemies, and filthy garments taken away
